sections.title: What KodaHosting is
sections.html:
KodaHosting turns an Android phone into a real Minecraft server. It's not a game client, and it's not a remote control talking to someone else's cloud box. The server process runs right on your phone, your world files live in your phone's storage, and the app wraps the whole thing in a clean control panel. Once you keep that in mind, pretty much every design decision in this codebase clicks into place, even the slightly unusual ones.

Under the hood, the system splits into three parts. Keeping them separate in your head makes troubleshooting a lot easier:

  • The device plane is the Android app itself. It downloads server jars and Java runtimes, starts and stops processes, streams the console, browses and edits files, runs backups, and applies config changes. Whenever something actually mutates your server, it happens here.
  • The connectivity plane is the tunnel. A bundled reverse proxy client forwards your Minecraft ports and web dashboard through a public server, so your friends can join cleanly without you touching router port forwarding or exposing your home IP.
  • The control plane is Supabase. It tracks which devices belong to which account, which servers exist, which ports are allocated, which app releases are live, and which extensions passed review. Every write runs through a server-side function that checks a per-device token.

There's also a fourth piece that's easy to overlook at first: KodaDash. It's a Java plugin running inside your Minecraft server that serves a web dashboard on port 7867. The Android app mirrors small JSON snapshots for stats, backups, and schedules into the server folder, and KodaDash reads them. That's how the web dashboard still shows sensible numbers even while your phone's screen is off and sleeping.

sections.title: Your own instance
sections.html:
The public repository gives you the full source code, but it obviously can't include a live production instance. Keys, accounts, domains, and operator admin tools stay private by design. Here's where the boundary sits:

Left out on purposeWhat it covers
secrets_local.hthe Supabase URL, public key, AI key, and tunnel host compiled into the native layer
The Supabase projectdatabase rows, storage buckets, auth users, and edge function secrets
Tunnel and DNS credentialsthe reverse proxy token and DNS provider keys used for custom domains
Signing materialthe release keystore, passwords, and Google Play credentials
The admin toolsthe operator web panel and the Kotlin admin app

One detail stays public intentionally: the imprint and privacy policy list a real operator and address. German law requires it, and honestly, a hosted service that hides who runs it isn't worth trusting anyway.

Spinning up your own instance

  1. Clone the repository and run an initial build with JDK 21.
  2. Create a Supabase project and apply the SQL files inside supabase/ in order: first migrations/, then security_fix_*.sql, and finally the remaining feature SQL (releases, extensions, notifications, KodaDash beta, and profile avatar). Each script reloads the API schema automatically.
  3. Set up the storage buckets: make artifacts, release_images, support_attachments, extension_assets, and avatars public, and keep extension_packages and data_exports private.
  4. Deploy the edge functions and configure their secrets. supabase/README.md documents the complete list. Don't skip get-tunnel-config, because the app calls it to pull its tunnel credentials.
  5. Run an frps server (vps-https/frps.toml.example gives you a hardened baseline) and drop its address along with your Supabase URL and public key into the native header file.
  6. Build a signed release APK and install it. On first launch, the app registers the device and creates the database row everything else attaches to.
  7. Optional: wire up the Discord release bot with your own bot token. The team admin panel and Android admin app aren't included in the public repo.
A brand-new instance starts empty on purpose. The app will still launch without a backend, but first-run device registration won't succeed and most cloud-backed screens will stay quiet.

sections.title: Building the app
sections.html:
The project is a single Gradle module paired with a small native layer that boots the embedded JVM. The first compile takes a few minutes while dependencies settle; incremental builds after that are fast.

export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk-21        # newer JDKs break the Gradle version in use
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug            # debug apk
./gradlew :app:assembleRelease -PKEYSTORE_PW=... -PKEY_PW=...
adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk
./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest        # unit tests, finishes in seconds

Watch out for signature mismatches: debug and release builds use different signing keys, so Android won't let you install one directly over the other. Pick which build type lives on your test phone early, or you'll have to uninstall and wipe local server data to switch.

Watch out for silent logs in release: release builds strip out all Android log calls, both in app code and framework wrappers. Logcat stays completely quiet in release mode, so never rely on it to debug a release APK. Surface diagnostics in the UI instead, or use the app's built-in debug log screen.

Target hardware is arm64 running Android 11 or newer. The APK only ships arm64 native libraries, so an x86 emulator won't be able to run servers.

sections.title: All screens at a glance
sections.html:
The app keeps its navigation flat: one home screen, one main server screen, and a focused set of setup flows and utility sheets around them. Here's the quick map:

ScreenWhat you do there

sections.title: Your servers, the home screen
sections.html:
Your home screen shows every server as a card with its name, server software, Minecraft version, and live status. Tap a card to open the full server screen, or long-press it for quick actions without leaving the list. Each card also puts the numbers you actually care about up front: player count, RAM usage, and uptime.

Hibernated servers appear dimmed with a one-tap wake button. When a server is mid-startup or shutting down, the button turns into an animated status indicator so you know it's working without having to open the console.

At the top of the screen, you'll find shortcuts to settings, support, Discord, the debug log, and the button to spin up a new server. Right above the list, a summary card adds up how many servers you have, how many are currently online, and how much memory they're using combined.

sections.title: Creating a server
sections.html:
The creation wizard walks you through one choice at a time in a fixed order, because choices like software type and version affect everything that comes after. You'll set the name and join address first, then pick your server software, Minecraft version, memory budget, and world configuration.

  • Server type: Paper, Purpur, Folia, and Vanilla if you want plugins or vanilla gameplay; Fabric, Forge, and NeoForge for mods; or PumpkinMC, a native server that runs without Java at all.
  • Minecraft version: filtered to versions that your chosen server software actually ships, complete with quick notes on plugin and mod compatibility.
  • Memory: the slider shows what your phone can safely spare alongside any other running servers.
  • World: configure world type, custom seed, or quick presets like a flat world for testing builds.
  • Setup mode: pick the Koda design to start with a tuned config and solid gameplay defaults, or choose a completely clean vanilla setup.

Once you finish the wizard, the app creates the server locally and registers it in the cloud. On its very first start, it automatically downloads the server jar and the matching Java runtime if needed, showing live progress right inside the console.

sections.title: The server dashboard tab
sections.html:
When you tap into a server, you land on the dashboard tab. It's built to answer three questions in two seconds: is everything healthy, who's playing right now, and what actions do I need?

Status and connectivity sit right at the top, with a copyable join address and a button to customize it. Below that, the player roster shows everyone online with their skins; tapping any player opens their full sheet with stats, live inventory, and moderation controls. CPU and RAM meters update in real time, and the quick-action bar lets you start, stop, or restart the server, automatically counting down in chat first if players are connected.

If your server ever crashes, the dashboard swaps in a crash card with a classified root cause, a concrete suggested fix, and the final lines of the log. Applying a suggested fix takes one tap and never makes blind guesses: it adjusts one specific known setting and tells you exactly what it changed.

sections.title: The console
sections.html:
The console streams raw server output live, strips out messy Minecraft ANSI colour codes, and highlights log levels so warnings and errors jump off the screen. Auto-scroll follows incoming lines until you scroll up to read something, then stays pinned right where you left it so you can actually read a stack trace in peace.

Just above the command bar sits a row of quick-command chips, and extensions can append their own chips there too. Anything you type goes straight to the server's stdin, so vanilla commands and plugin commands both work exactly as expected.

  • Copy puts the visible console buffer on your clipboard, ready to paste into a support ticket.
  • Log opens the app's own verbose log, which is where you look if a runtime download or tunnel startup fails before Minecraft even boots.
  • AI crash analysis can walk through a crash log with you, and always asks for explicit consent before sending a single line off your phone.

sections.title: Files: browse, edit, unpack, export
sections.html:
The files tab gives you a full file manager rooted at your server directory. Tap folders to navigate, tap text files to open the built-in editor, or long-press any item to rename, copy, cut, delete, or share it.

  • Import pulls files in from anywhere Android's file picker can see, including local storage, other apps, and cloud drives.
  • Unpack here extracts ZIP and RAR archives right in place. If a RAR archive is password-protected, the app tells you plainly instead of failing silently.
  • Export zips the entire server directory into your Downloads folder without an extra wrapper folder, so you can re-import it directly later.
  • NBT viewer lets you inspect binary NBT files like player data and level.dat as a clean, readable tree (read-only on purpose so nothing gets corrupted).

The built-in text editor handles files up to 1 MB with clean formatting for properties, JSON, and YAML. If you hit save while the server is still online, it reminds you that many config files are only read at startup.

sections.title: Mods and plugins
sections.html:
Mods and plugins live in their own tab, complete with a built-in Modrinth browser. You can search, filter automatically by your server's software and Minecraft version, install with a tap, and update with a tap.

Your installed list pulls metadata directly out of each jar (name, version, authors, and icon) and falls back to Modrinth when a jar doesn't bundle its own icon. Flipping a toggle disables a jar cleanly by renaming it rather than deleting it, and removing a jar moves it to trash for a while first in case you change your mind.

Don't mix up server jars and app extensions. This tab manages plugins and mods running inside Minecraft. App extensions customize the KodaHosting app itself and are covered later in these docs.

sections.title: Starting, stopping, restarting
sections.html:
Starting a server looks like a single tap, but a lot happens behind the curtain: the app checks your phone's free RAM and network budget, gets the right runtime ready, writes any generated config files, launches the process, and watches the console for the startup completion line before flipping the status to online.

Stopping always tries the graceful route first. It tells the server to save the world and shut down cleanly, and only terminates the process if it stops responding. A force-kill option is available when a server is truly hung, tucked behind a confirmation dialog because killing a JVM mid-write can corrupt chunks.

Restarts go through the exact same graceful stop sequence so nobody loses inventory or builds. If players are online when you trigger a restart, the app broadcasts a countdown warning in chat first.

sections.title: Changing the Minecraft version
sections.html:
You can change a server's Minecraft version from the dashboard settings wheel. Because shifting versions touches world formats and plugin compatibility, the app treats it as a real migration rather than a casual toggle. Only versions officially published for your current server software appear in the list.

  • Upgrades strongly recommend taking a backup first, though you can choose to skip it.
  • Downgrades require a backup before continuing, since Minecraft worlds and chunks aren't backwards-compatible.
  • Your previous server jar stays safely in place until the new version boots cleanly.

Plugins and mods won't auto-migrate across major Minecraft updates. Once the switch finishes, the app nudges you to check the mods/plugins tab, where Modrinth update checks usually locate matching builds right away.

sections.title: Backups and restore
sections.html:
Backups are standard ZIP snapshots of your entire server folder stored alongside the app, and they're the fastest way to make sure a bad plugin or accidental TNT mishap stays a minor inconvenience. You can trigger a backup manually whenever you want, or set up automatic backups on stop, daily, or both.

  • Keep count sets how many backups to retain before older snapshots rotate out.
  • Restore rolls your server folder back to the selected archive while keeping your current files safe until the restore finishes cleanly.
  • Size and age appear on every backup entry so freeing up storage is an informed choice rather than guesswork.
You can only restore a backup while the server is stopped. The app enforces that strictly, and it has saved plenty of worlds from half-written corruption.

sections.title: Automations and schedules
sections.html:
The automation sheet lets you schedule recurring chores: restart, stop, save the world, broadcast a chat announcement, or run any console command. Tasks can repeat on an interval or run daily at a specific clock time, and you can optionally tell a task to wait until the server is empty.

Most hosts start with a nightly restart paired with a chat warning a few minutes beforehand. When an empty-only restart is queued, the app announces it in chat so nobody gets caught off guard. Everything you configure here is mirrored into the server folder so KodaDash displays the exact same schedule list in the browser.

sections.title: Players, stats and moderation
sections.html:
Player management covers both sides of your community: who's connected right now and everyone who has joined in the past. Tap any player to pull up their skin, total playtime, gameplay stats, and a live inventory view read directly from their save data.

  • Live actions: kick, ban, pardon, op/deop, private message, gamemode switch, teleport, and XP adjustments.
  • Care actions: heal, feed, saturate, plus a full inventory wipe guarded by a double confirmation.
  • Inventory editing: drag items straight between slots to rearrange a player's inventory, written right back into their player data.
  • Whitelist: toggle server-wide whitelist enforcement and add or remove individual players using the server's native whitelist rules.

sections.title: The MOTD editor
sections.html:
Your MOTD is the two-line banner players see in their Minecraft multiplayer list, and writing colour codes by hand is nobody's idea of fun. The built-in editor gives you formatting buttons for colours, bold, italic, underline, obfuscated text, resets, and hex colours in all three formats Minecraft accepts.

Each toolbar button drops the right code at your cursor without losing your typing position, while a live preview shows how it will look in-game. If you'd rather edit the raw text directly, the plain server.properties view is still right there in the files tab.

Tip: drag the bottom edge of the MOTD input box to resize it when you're crafting longer messages on a smaller screen.

sections.title: Resource packs
sections.html:
You don't need an external file host to serve a custom resource pack. Pick a ZIP from your phone, and the app handles every step: copies it into the server folder, calculates its SHA-1 checksum, updates the pack URL and hash in server.properties, and lets you flip the required-pack toggle on or off.

KodaDash serves the pack straight over your tunnel on your server's join address, so players download it automatically on connect. The dashboard shows whether a resource pack is active and how big the download is.

sections.title: World settings: type, seed, gameplay
sections.html:
World type, seed, gamemode, difficulty, view and simulation distance, spawn protection, and hardcore mode all live in the settings tab and write directly to server.properties. After saving, the app reads the file back and compares values so any manual edits you made in the text editor never get silently clobbered.

If you tweak server.properties by hand while the server is offline, the app spots the mismatch next time you open settings and asks which version you want to keep. That way the UI and the config file never drift out of sync.

sections.title: Memory settings
sections.html:
Every server gets its own JVM heap limit, and the app keeps an eye on the global ceiling. Android always needs breathing room for itself, so if you launch a second server, the RAM slider automatically caps itself to what's actually free and warns you before pushing the phone into heavy swapping.

Because heap size is passed as a JVM launch flag, changing it takes effect on the next restart. The app also feeds your device's real memory budget into crash diagnostics, so if a server runs out of memory, the recommended fix suggests a realistic number for your specific phone rather than a generic guess.

sections.title: Java runtimes
sections.html:
Different Minecraft versions require different Java versions, and bundling all of them inside the APK would make it massive. Instead, KodaHosting downloads the exact runtime a server needs on demand (covering everything from JDK 25 down to Java 17 and Java 8) and remembers that preference per server.

  • Automatic picks the right JDK for your server software and Minecraft version.
  • Manual lets you pin a specific runtime, which is handy if a legacy mod refuses to run on anything newer than Java 17.
  • Fallback keeps your server bootable if a selected runtime is broken, clearly telling you which fallback it used and why.

Runtime downloads stream their progress into the console tab. Downloaded runtimes are shared across all servers on your phone, so spinning up a second server on the same Java version is much faster.

sections.title: Hibernate and wake
sections.html:
Hibernation puts a server to sleep without deleting your work. The app stops the process, releases the join address on the tunnel, packs up the server folder, and leaves a clean marker so your home screen shows a sleeping server instead of a missing one.

When you're ready to play again, waking it unpacks the folder, grabs a fresh join address, and boots the server right back up. A hibernated server consumes zero RAM, zero battery, and zero tunnel bandwidth, which makes a big difference if you juggle several worlds on one phone.

Device-to-device server transfers use the exact same archive format under the hood, which is why both features share the same packing pipeline.

sections.title: MariaDB and Redis
sections.html:
Running plugins that expect a real database? KodaHosting can run MariaDB or Redis right alongside your Minecraft server on the same phone, using credentials you pick in the setup wizard. Both run as native binaries from the same runtime stack, so there's nothing extra to install.

The database card displays everything your plugin config needs (port, username, and generated password), and the data directory sits right beside the server files so normal backups capture both together. If you see the Database server type on the main list, that's simply a standalone MariaDB or Redis instance running without a Minecraft server attached.

sections.title: Tunnel and join addresses
sections.html:
Most phones sit behind carrier NAT or a home router where outside players can't connect directly. To solve that, KodaHosting bundles a reverse proxy client that forwards your Minecraft ports and web dashboard through a public relay server. Players connect using the join address shown on your dashboard, which follows the tunnel rather than your home IP.

Tunnel credentials aren't baked into the APK. Instead, the app requests them from the backend on demand, caches them for a few hours, and refreshes them quietly in the background. If a tunnel token expires, it heals itself automatically without you ever having to reinstall the app.

  • Join address is assigned automatically when you create a server, and you can change it once per day.
  • Java and Bedrock ports both forward automatically whenever Bedrock crossplay is enabled.
  • KodaDash rides through the same tunnel on its own reserved port band.

sections.title: Custom domains
sections.html:
If you already own a domain, the custom domain wizard walks you through pointing it at your server with an SRV record. It hands you the exact record values, lets you copy them with one tap, and checks public DNS until the record propagates. You don't need to be a DNS expert; the wizard explains what each record does along the way.

Since DNS propagation can take a little while, you can close the wizard and come back later. Your default join address keeps working in the meantime, and you can unlink your custom domain from the same card whenever you want to switch back.

sections.title: Ports and network
sections.html:
Every server gets two paired ports managed automatically by the app: the local port Minecraft binds to on the phone, and the public port exposed through the tunnel. KodaDash always uses a separate reserved port range so it never bumps into a game server.

You can inspect every active and free port right from the dashboard. If another app on your phone is already holding a port, startup stops with a clear explanation and a suggested fix instead of throwing a cryptic crash.

sections.title: Network budgets and the network alarm
sections.html:
Hosting on a phone usually means sharing Wi-Fi or mobile data with everyone else in the house. KodaHosting tracks per-server bandwidth in real time and lets you put sensible guardrails around it.

  • Budget rules cap transfer speeds and split bandwidth across servers so one busy world doesn't choke the rest.
  • The network alarm alerts you when the shared tunnel relay starts getting heavy load, ideally before players feel any lag.
  • Protection mode steps in to stop servers when the network is genuinely overloaded and explains why, rather than letting everyone rubber-band.

sections.title: The KodaDash web dashboard
sections.html:
KodaDash is a lightweight Java plugin bundled inside your Minecraft server that exposes a web interface over the tunnel. It solves a super practical problem: managing your server from a laptop or browser when you don't have your phone in your hand.

TabWhat you get
Overviewlive status, online players, RAM usage, TPS history, and info about the phone hosting the server
Consolelive streaming console with scrollback history and log-level filtering
Playersplayer list with live inventories, stats, and moderation tools
Filesbrowse and edit server files right in your browser
Pluginsview installed jars, toggle them on or off, and search Modrinth
Settingsedit server.properties while preserving existing comments

KodaDash uses its own access token and optional password. One deliberate safety choice: the backups tab is strictly read-only, so even if someone ever leaked a dashboard token, they couldn't wipe out your only world backups.

sections.title: MCP for AI clients
sections.html:
Starting with KodaDash 1.2.0, your server exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Any AI client that speaks remote MCP can inspect server status, read logs and config files, run console commands, and tweak settings without you needing the phone app open. It connects directly to standard MCP clients rather than locking you into an in-app chat box.

Before you start

  • A running Paper or Purpur server with KodaDash enabled.
  • KodaHosting v0.147beta / version code 8527 or newer (that build bundles the KodaDash 1.1.0 jar and newer updates).
  • Your HTTPS dashboard URL, such as https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/. Your MCP endpoint is simply that same host with /mcp added.

Enable MCP

  1. In KodaDash, head to Settings, AI access (MCP). Inside the Android app, open your server and go to KodaDash, AI access (MCP).
  2. Open Connection and switch on Enable MCP. KodaDash generates a dedicated MCP token for you.
  3. Copy both the endpoint URL and the token. Your endpoint looks like https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp.

Your MCP token is completely separate from your KodaDash login token and your KodaHosting account password. It only grants access to this single server and only to the specific tool groups you switch on.

You'll also find built-in How to set up and Troubleshooting rows right inside the app's MCP sheet, so you can grab these steps offline without opening the docs.

Connect an AI client

Every MCP client asks for the same three ingredients: the endpoint URL, your Bearer token, and the HTTP transport. Only the config file path and key names vary. The table below gives you the quick cheat sheet, followed by copy-paste examples. Even faster: tap Copy JSON in the app's Connection sheet to copy a ready-to-paste mcpServers block.

ClientConfig locationFields to set
ZCodeMCP server list, New MCP serverType HTTP, URL, Headers JSON
Codex~/.codex/config.toml[mcp_servers.…], url, bearer_token_env_var
Antigravity~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.jsonserverUrl, headers
Claude Code.mcp.json or claude mcp add-jsontype: http, url, headers
Cursor~/.cursor/mcp.json or .cursor/mcp.jsonurl, headers
VS Code.vscode/mcp.json or user mcp.jsonservers, type: http, url, headers
Windsurf~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.jsonserverUrl, headers
Claude DesktopConnectors or a stdio bridgeOAuth, or mcp-remote for a static Bearer header

ZCode

  1. Open the MCP server list and pick New MCP server.
  2. Name: kodahosting-your-server. Scope: This computer or User.
  3. Type: HTTP. Timeout MS: 30000. Protocol version: Auto.
  4. URL: https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp.
  5. Headers: {"Authorization": "Bearer <mcp-token>"} in either the Form or JSON tab.
  6. Save. Your KodaDash tools should pop up in the client's tool list right away.

30000 ms works well for most phones; bump it to 60000 if your device takes a bit longer to wake up. Leave Protocol version on Auto.

Codex

[mcp_servers.kodahosting]
url = "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp"
bearer_token_env_var = "KODA_MCP_TOKEN"

Set the token in the shell environment where you launch Codex rather than putting it straight into the TOML file: export KODA_MCP_TOKEN=<mcp-token>. You can also register it via CLI with codex mcp add kodahosting --url https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp --bearer-token-env-var KODA_MCP_TOKEN. If you really need a static header in the file, use [mcp_servers.kodahosting.http_headers] with Authorization = "Bearer ...", though the environment variable is much safer.

Antigravity

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "serverUrl": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <mcp-token>" }
    }
  }
}

Note that Antigravity expects serverUrl rather than url. Put this in ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json globally, or .agents/mcp_config.json inside a workspace. Via CLI: agy mcp add --type http --header "Authorization: Bearer <mcp-token>" kodahosting https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp.

Claude Code

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}

Save this to .mcp.json or pass it to claude mcp add-json kodahosting '{...}'. Keep in mind Claude Code reads exported shell environment variables and does not automatically load a plain .env file.

Cursor

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}

Works in either your global ~/.cursor/mcp.json or a project-level .cursor/mcp.json. Cursor automatically picks up Streamable HTTP from the url field.

VS Code

{
  "inputs": [
    { "type": "promptString", "id": "koda-mcp-token", "description": "KodaHosting MCP token", "password": true }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:koda-mcp-token}" }
    }
  }
}

Heads up: VS Code uses servers at the top level instead of mcpServers. Drop this into .vscode/mcp.json or open your user config via MCP: Open User Configuration in the Command Palette.

Windsurf

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "serverUrl": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}

Windsurf specifically looks for serverUrl; pasting a snippet with url can fail silently. Hit refresh in the MCP panel after saving.

Claude Desktop

Claude Desktop's built-in custom connector mainly targets public or OAuth servers, and not every build exposes custom request headers. If your version lets you enter a header, use that. Otherwise, bridge it locally over stdio with mcp-remote:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kodahosting": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp",
               "--header", "Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER}"],
      "env": { "AUTH_HEADER": "Bearer <mcp-token>" }
    }
  }
}

If you're on Windows, keep the space inside AUTH_HEADER and pass Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER} so the argument doesn't get split on whitespace. Note that mcp-remote is an external tool and isn't bundled with KodaDash.

Using another client?

Start with the standard mcpServers layout using url and headers. If your client asks for a transport type, select HTTP or Streamable HTTP. If it expects serverUrl instead of url, swap the key name. If it only speaks stdio, put an HTTP-to-stdio bridge in front.

Quick test with curl

curl -s https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <mcp-token>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'

If everything is wired up right, you'll get back a JSON response with a tools array. Seeing a 405 on GET /mcp is completely expected: the endpoint accepts POST requests only and doesn't run an SSE stream.

Consolerun commands as the console sender (excluding start, stop, restart, and hibernate)
Fileslist, read, write, rename, create directories, and delete. Files up to 16 MB go through files_push in one request; larger jars are assembled in ≤16 MB base64 chunks with files_chunk_append onto a .part name and swapped onto their final path with files_replace_atomic, so a failed transfer never leaves a half-written jar behind
Serverread and edit server.properties, plus validated single-setting helpers for MOTD, max players, difficulty, gamemode, PvP, whitelist, online-mode, view distance, simulation distance, and spawn protection
Pluginslist, enable, disable, install from a public HTTPS URL, search Modrinth, and install compatible Modrinth versions with SHA-512 verification

An AI client can never start, stop, restart, or hibernate your server. Power controls stay strictly in human hands inside the app or dashboard, and KodaDash rejects those commands even if an AI tries sending them through the console.

Dedicated helper tools include mcp_status, modrinth_search, modrinth_install, server_setting, and the big-file helpers files_push, files_chunk_append, and files_replace_atomic. The tools/list call always reflects the exact tool set of the installed KodaDash version, so newer plugins can add tools without a config change on your side.

Security guardrails

  • Read-only mode hides every write tool completely. Great when you just want an AI to diagnose a lag spike or inspect logs.
  • Capability switches let you independently toggle console commands, file writes, server.properties edits, plugin actions, and Modrinth downloads.
  • Regenerate invalidates your current MCP token on the spot and issues a fresh one. Just remember to update your AI client config afterward.
  • Destructive actions (and overwriting existing files) require an explicit confirm:true flag. Modrinth installs always check the SHA-512 hash against version metadata and delete the file immediately on mismatch.
  • Modrinth lookups and downloads are locked strictly to api.modrinth.com and cdn.modrinth.com over HTTPS; private, loopback, and reserved IP ranges are blocked.
  • Every single tool call gets logged to plugins/KodaDash/mcp-audit.log, with file contents and any argument names containing password, secret, or token automatically redacted.
  • plugins/KodaDash/config.yml, the audit log itself, and .frpc.toml are completely off-limits to MCP file tools.
  • Treat your MCP token like a root password. Anyone holding it can invoke whichever tools you've enabled, so keep it out of public repos and screenshots.

What context the AI receives

When a client connects, KodaDash sends an initial system prompt giving the AI practical context: KodaHosting environment details, server software and version, loaded worlds, plugins, live players and TPS, plus your phone's model, Android version, RAM, battery, and free storage. It also reinforces the ground rules: never start or stop the server, ask before destructive changes, never expose tokens, and prefer read-only checks.

Software and version data reported by the running server are treated as authoritative. The app/cloud mirror in server-info.json is explicitly tagged as secondary and potentially stale, so an outdated cloud server_version is never mistaken for reality. Even if an AI client drops the initial prompt later, it can pull the exact same snapshot anytime with the read-only server_context tool.

Troubleshooting

SymptomWhat to check
404Either MCP or KodaDash is turned off. Both need to be enabled for the endpoint to exist.
401Your token is mistyped or was rotated. Copy the active token from Connection.
405 on GETExpected behavior. Send POST requests; SSE isn't used here.
No connectionMake sure the server is online and your HTTPS dashboard loads normally at https://<server>/.
Tools are missingRead-only mode or a specific capability switch is turned off under Permissions.
Old pluginKodaDash updates when the app launches the server. Update to build 8527 or newer and restart the server once.

If an AI ever does something surprising, open plugins/KodaDash/mcp-audit.log first. It records the exact tool called, redacted arguments, outcome, and duration for every request.

sections.title: Bedrock crossplay
sections.html:
Want friends on consoles, tablets, or phones to join your Java world? Turning on Bedrock crossplay installs Geyser and Floodgate, generates configs pre-matched to your server setup, and forwards the extra UDP port Bedrock expects.

If you're running PumpkinMC, Bedrock support is native to the server itself, so it's just a built-in toggle. Either way, your dashboard displays both join details cleanly: the Java address and the Bedrock address with its port.

sections.title: Voice chat
sections.html: Enabling Simple Voice Chat installs the right plugin or mod for your server software, opens the extra UDP port over the tunnel, and writes out the voice chat config with the proper public port and address. Both Java and Bedrock players get working proximity voice without you having to rent a separate server.

sections.title: Your account
sections.html:
You don't need an account to host servers on KodaHosting. Creating one is completely optional, and it unlocks the web dashboard, server recovery when you switch phones, and family sharing permissions.

You can sign in with email and password or with Google. Notice the direction of trust: your account links to your device, not the other way around. Your local device token remains the credential that authorizes writes, and it never leaves your phone.

sections.title: Linking a Minecraft account
sections.html:
Linking proves a Minecraft username belongs to you, which powers the lobby and the /join command. The app gives you a short verification code; hop into the lobby server, run /link with that code, and your Minecraft profile appears right on your account card.

One Minecraft account can only be linked to one device at a time. If you move it to a new phone, the old device loses the link deliberately so shared setups don't drift out of sync.

sections.title: Your nickname
sections.html: Your nickname is what other players see in the public server list and lobby instead of an internal device ID. The app asks you to pick one after first launch (and gently reminds you at most once a day when opening social screens), and you can update it anytime in settings.

sections.title: Moving servers to a new device
sections.html:
Upgrading your phone doesn't mean starting your worlds over. Device transfer moves an entire server directly from one phone to another over your local Wi-Fi, encrypted end to end. The old phone packs and serves the archive, the new phone pulls it down and adopts it, and your join addresses come along for the ride.

  • Pairing works either by picking the nearby device or entering an 8-character code, and the receiving phone always shows a confirmation prompt naming the sender.
  • Encryption uses an ephemeral key that only exists for that transfer window, keeping your world files unreadable even on a shared network.
  • Safe cleanup only runs after the receiving phone confirms everything arrived intact. If your Wi-Fi drops halfway through, your original copy is untouched.

sections.title: Family accounts and permissions
sections.html:
One main account can own several servers while letting friends or family help run them with granular permissions. You decide per person who can start, stop, hibernate, delete, manage players, install plugins, or send console commands, all controlled with simple switches while the main account stays in full control.

Because everyone signs in with their own account, permissions follow the person rather than a specific phone. Need to revoke access? Flip a single switch and it takes effect on their very next action.

sections.title: KodaCluster
sections.html:
Got a spare Android phone sitting in a drawer? Connect two phones with a USB cable to turn them into a mini hosting cluster. One phone acts as the master controller, showing a unified dashboard for both devices and starting or stopping servers on the secondary phone. They talk over a tiny JSON protocol straight across USB, so it doesn't even depend on Wi-Fi.

Set the secondary phone to USB file transfer mode. The USB accessory filter is already built into the app manifest, so the cluster links up automatically without manual pairing.

sections.title: Tickets and bug reports
sections.html:
You can reach support without leaving the app: write a subject and message, attach screenshots or logs if they help, and follow the full reply thread in one place. Bug reports and server reports feed into the exact same ticket system with a quicker form, so nothing slips through the cracks.

Opening a ticket requires an account so replies actually have somewhere to go. Your ticket list tracks the live status of every thread and keeps the full conversation history.

sections.title: The personal chat
sections.html:
Alongside regular support tickets, there's a direct, end-to-end encrypted chat with the developer. Your phone generates the keys locally, the private key never leaves your device, and every message is encrypted with ECDH and AES-GCM before it's ever stored.

On the other end, only the developer can decrypt messages using a key stored behind a PIN in a separate admin app. The whole idea is simple: honest conversations stay strictly between two people, and nobody in the middle, not even the database storing the ciphertext, can read them.

sections.title: The help screen
sections.html:
If something during a session signals that someone might be going through a really hard time, the app shows a calm, quiet screen with one goal: reminding you that someone cares and offering real ways to reach out, including crisis hotlines, youth chat support, and the personal chat.

It never blocks your access, never reports anything anywhere, and never touches your servers. Dismissing it only has a brief pause so it doesn't get tapped away by accident. It's in the app simply because the people using this software are real people, and the person building it is too.

sections.title: Bans and enforcement
sections.html:
Bans are always a last resort, and the app treats them that way. Server names get checked up front, abuse reports are reviewed by a real human, and if a server does get banned, the screen clearly explains why and lets you download a backup of your world instead of stranding your data.

Device bans only exist for persistent abuse that tries to survive reinstalls. They're rare, and the checks behind them are deliberately narrow: tampering with the app's own protected state or forging device identities, and nothing else.

sections.title: What extensions are
sections.html:
Extensions let anyone add new screens, translations, themes, settings entries, and server tabs to KodaHosting without forking the app or waiting on an official update. Each extension is just a ZIP file containing a manifest and, if it has a UI, a lightweight web view. Zero native code is ever loaded dynamically, which keeps the app compliant with Play Store rules and ensures a buggy extension can't crash the app around it.

The quickest way to learn is to peek at the working examples right in the repository:

  • Koda Lab, an interactive test bench that exercises every bridge call and prints raw responses
  • Live Log, a clean custom screen in roughly a hundred lines
  • Polski, a real production language pack
  • Ocean, a custom colour theme combined with UI tweaks
  • The written reference, along with the full JSON schema right beside it

sections.title: Package format
sections.html:
my-extension.kodaext          (a ZIP, files at the root)
  manifest.json                required
  ui/index.html                required when the extension has a screen
  ui/app.js, ui/style.css      your interface
  lang/es.json                 language packs you contribute
  automations.json             automation rules
  icon.png                     128x128, shown in the hub

Here's a kitchen-sink manifest that touches almost every feature. Treat it like a menu and strip out whatever your extension doesn't need:

{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "eu.example.mypack",
  "name": "My Pack",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "versionCode": 1,
  "author": "Your name",
  "description": "What it does, in one sentence.",
  "license": "GPL-3.0-or-later",
  "source_url": "https://github.com/you/mypack",
  "minAppVersion": 8514,
  "permissions": ["servers.read", "console.read", "storage", "http:discord.com"],
  "ui": { "entry": "ui/index.html", "title": "My Pack" },
  "contributes": {
    "languages": [ { "code": "es", "name": "Espanol", "file": "lang/es.json" } ],
    "themes": [ { "id": "ocean", "name": "Ocean", "color": "#006874" } ],
    "settings": [ { "title": "My Pack", "subtitle": "Open the panel", "target": "overview" } ],
    "server_tabs": [ { "id": "panel", "title": "Panel", "target": "server" } ],
    "ui": { "hide": ["btn_github_main"], "console_chips": ["/tps", "time set day"] }
  },
  "automations": "automations.json"
}
FieldRule
schemamust be 1
idlowercase reverse-domain identifier, at least two dot-separated segments, max 64 characters
namemax 48 characters, displayed in the extension hub
version and versionCodeversionCode must strictly increase with every update
licenserequired; shown right beside the extension in the app
source_urlrecommended; displayed as a clickable source link
minAppVersionminimum KodaHosting build number required to install
permissionscapabilities your code needs, enforced by the bridge
contributeslanguages, themes, settings rows, server tabs, and UI tweaks added to the app

sections.title: The bridge API
sections.html:
Every extension screen runs inside a sandboxed WebView that can only access its own package files. To interact with KodaHosting, your page calls a single global object, window.koda, which the app injects before your scripts execute. Every method returns a Promise resolving to a plain JSON object, and errors come back as an object with an error property instead of throwing unhandled exceptions.

const { servers } = await koda.servers.list();
const first = servers[0];
const { lines } = await koda.console.tail(first.id, 200);

await koda.storage.set('lastServer', first.id);
const saved = await koda.storage.get('lastServer');   // { value: '...' }

const theme = await koda.theme();    // colours, so your page can match the app
const { lang } = await koda.locale();
koda.ui.toast('Hello from my pack');
const { ok } = await koda.ui.confirm('Restart?', 'Players will be kicked.');
CallWhat it returns
koda.api, koda.versionbridge version info so you can gracefully handle older app builds
koda.servers.list(), get(id)servers with a stable schema: id, name, type, mcVersion, state, port, address, ramMB, maxPlayers
koda.console.tail(id, lines)recent console lines, up to 1,000 lines
koda.storage.get/set/remove/keysprivate key-value storage scoped to your extension (1 MB limit)
koda.ui.toast, koda.ui.confirmnative toast and confirmation dialog styled to match the app
koda.theme(), koda.locale()active app palette and language code so your UI blends right in

Permissions

Declare everything you need in manifest.json. The app enforces permissions at runtime, so calling koda.servers.list() without servers.read simply returns an error object.

PermissionCurrent status
storage, servers.read, console.readlive today
console.send, servers.controldeclared, next phase (gated by in-app confirmation)
players.read, players.actions, files.read, notificationsdeclared, next phase
http:hostscoped outbound HTTP access for one specific domain
Only read permissions and storage are active right now. Install Koda Lab on your device to inspect the exact live payload every bridge call returns on your build, rather than guessing.

sections.title: Language packs
sections.html:
// lang/es.json, the keys are the app's string resource names
{
  "tab_dashboard": "Panel",
  "jars_title": "MODS Y PLUGINS",
  "sd_toast_log_copied": "Registro copiado",
  "ext_ui_chips_count": "%1$d comandos extra en la consola."
}

Language packs don't have to translate every single string in the app. Anything you omit falls back cleanly to the user's current language, so even a partial pack is immediately useful and easy to expand over time. Just be careful with format placeholders like %1$s or %1$d: keep them verbatim, because a missing or extra placeholder will crash Android when that string formats.

python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py path/to/lang/es.json

Run that checker before shipping. It validates every key against the app's actual string resources and flags typos that would otherwise sit silently unused. Users apply a language pack from the extension's action sheet (requiring a quick restart), and disabling the extension automatically restores their previous language.

sections.title: Themes, including full palettes
sections.html:
"themes": [
  { "id": "ocean", "name": "Ocean", "color": "#006874" },
  { "id": "midnight", "name": "Midnight", "color": "#00D9FF",
    "colors": { "primary": "#00D9FF", "surface": "#07070F", "card": "#14141F",
                "text": "#EDEDF5", "text_dim": "#8C8C9C", "error": "#FF4455" } }
]

Supplying just color gives the app a seed colour to feed into its Material 3 engine, generating a harmonious palette across buttons, cards, and highlights automatically. If you want total visual control, add a colors object with any combination of primary, surface, card, text, text_dim, outline, online, and error. The app overrides the generated roles with yours and computes readable contrast colours for text on top of your accents.

Contributed themes show up in two places on purpose: inside the extension's action sheet and in Settings, Appearance, Themes. Each theme gets its own toggle, and enabling one automatically switches off whichever theme was active before.

App theme modeHow your theme applies
Material 3 moderestyles the entire UI by resolving colour roles across the view tree
Classic designmaps your accent, surfaces, cards, text, and outlines onto the classic palette slots

sections.title: Settings entries
sections.html:
"settings": [
  { "title": "My Pack", "subtitle": "Everything in one screen", "target": "overview" }
]

Settings entries appear right beneath the extension hub inside the app's Settings screen. Each row automatically gets a small info icon displaying the extension name, version, author, and license so users always know what's built-in and what comes from an extension.

Tapping a row opens your UI with #target appended to the URL, making it easy to deep-link straight to a specific sub-view. Each extension can contribute up to four settings rows.

sections.title: Server tabs
sections.html:
"server_tabs": [ { "id": "panel", "title": "Panel", "target": "server" } ]

This adds your own custom tab to every server's detail screen. When opened, the app passes the active server ID in the URL hash, like #server&server=the-server-id, so your page knows exactly which server the user is looking at. Grabbing it takes two lines of JavaScript:

const parts = location.hash.replace('#', '').split('&');
const server = (parts.find(p => p.startsWith('server=')) || '').split('=')[1];
One honest caveat: the optional sleek layout doesn't have a shared tab container, so contributed server tabs are skipped there. Extensions can add up to four server tabs each.

sections.title: Interface tweaks
sections.html:
"ui": {
  "hide": ["btn_github_main"],
  "console_chips": ["/tps", "/list", "time set day"]
}

hide removes specific UI elements by their Android view IDs, while console_chips adds custom quick-command buttons right above the server console input. Both take effect automatically whenever the extension is enabled, without any extra toggles to dig for.

sections.title: Automations
sections.html:
{
  "schema": 1,
  "automations": [
    { "id": "crash-watch", "name": "Crash warning",
      "when": { "type": "log_match", "server": "*", "pattern": "(?i)(crash|exception)" },
      "then": [ { "type": "notify", "title": "Crash on {server}", "text": "{line}" },
                { "type": "http", "method": "POST",
                  "url": "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...", "body": { "content": "{line}" } } ] }
  ]
}

Automation rules pair a trigger (server state changes, regex log matches, or schedules) with a list of actions (notifications, webhooks, or console commands). Template variables like {server} and {line} expand automatically when a rule fires.

The schema is finalized and validated at install time today, while the background rule runner lands in the next phase. You can already ship valid automations.json definitions in your packages now.

sections.title: Packaging and testing
sections.html:
# validate the manifest and build the package
python3 extensions/tools/pack_extension.py extensions/examples/koda-lab

# check a language pack before you ship it
python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py my/pack/lang/es.json

Both scripts enforce the exact same validation checks the Android app runs. Catching an unknown view ID, missing translation file, malformed hex colour, or stagnant version code on your laptop is a lot nicer than hitting it on someone's phone.

To test locally, sideload your package via Settings, Extensions, + and pick the file. Updating an extension preserves its saved storage; uninstalling clears storage cleanly. You'll also find a Reload action in the hub menu so you can iterate without reinstalling every time.

sections.title: The store and the API
sections.html:
The extension store lives at host.kodanetwork.eu/store and mirrors straight into the app's extension hub under Discover. You publish on the website, users install inside the app, and both sides speak to the same public API.

Submitting

Sign in with your KodaHosting account, pick your .kodaext archive, enter the name, version, license, and source URL, and hit submit. Your browser computes the SHA-256 hash and the backend verifies it after upload, inspecting the manifest inside the archive and rejecting anything with an invalid ID, version code, license, or permission set. Every submission goes through human review first, and the first approved release puts your extension live in the catalog.

Every submission sits in one of five clear states: PENDING while waiting for review, APPROVED once live, REJECTED with a written reason, DELISTED if pulled down after publication, or WITHDRAWN if you cancelled it yourself. Your developer dashboard shows both the state and any review note so nothing ever disappears silently.

New versions

Pushing an update follows the same review flow. While your new build is pending, the store keeps serving the previous approved version so an unreviewed or broken upload never breaks existing installs. When a user updates, the new package installs cleanly over the old one while keeping all stored extension data.

The API

Everything powering the website and app is served from https://api.kodanetwork.eu. Public read endpoints don't require an API key:

GET /v1/status                    live numbers (servers, players, store, tunnel server)
GET /v1/releases                  published app releases
GET /v1/servers                   the public server directory (name, status, players, MOTD, owner)
GET /v1/servers/{host}?ping=1     one server: owner, and a live minecraft ping (players, MOTD, favicon)
GET /v1/extensions                the catalog, approved only, with the newest version
GET /v1/extensions?author=Name    everything one publisher released
GET /v1/extensions/{id}           one extension with all approved versions
GET /v1/extensions/{id}/download  redirects to a 60 second signed url

Authenticated routes expect your Supabase session access token as a Bearer header (the exact same login the web dashboard uses):

GET   /v1/me                        profile, nickname, avatar url, counters, 2FA state
PATCH /v1/me                        nickname and avatar
POST  /v1/me/avatar                 upload target for a profile picture
GET   /v1/me/devices                linked devices with their telemetry and MC accounts
POST  /v1/me/devices/{id}/unlink    detach a device; the app keeps working standalone
GET   /v1/me/extensions             your submissions with their review state
GET   /v1/me/tickets                your support tickets
POST  /v1/me/tickets/{id}/messages  reply to a ticket from the browser

When a public server is reachable, the detail endpoint performs a real Minecraft server-list ping and returns live players, MOTD, and server favicon (cached for one minute). Public listings only ever expose the owner's linked Minecraft username, never app UUIDs, tokens, or hardware IDs.

Two things stay off the public API deliberately: the personal support chat is end-to-end encrypted between the Android app and admin app, so it only lives inside the app. And extension packages never get static public URLs; every download redirects to a signed link that expires after 60 seconds, keeping pending or rejected uploads unreachable.

All routes sit behind database-backed sliding-window rate limits (120 reads per minute per IP, 30 writes, 90 per account, and 20 for ticket replies and uploads), shared consistently across edge instances. If you hit a limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and the site displays a calm cooldown screen with a countdown instead of throwing cryptic errors.

sections.title: Translations
sections.html:
Every piece of UI copy lives in app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml, with built-in translations right alongside it in values-de, values-zh-rCN, and values-pl. Because Android falls back to the default file for any missing entry, you can start with a partial translation and fill in the rest over time.

Adding a new built-in language just means creating its resource directory and wiring it into the language picker in settings. Two scripts keep everything safe:

python3 extensions/tools/check_translation.py app/src/main/res/values-pl/strings.xml
python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py path/to/lang/es.json
Always run the checker after editing strings. A broken format placeholder looks totally innocent in XML, then crashes the app at runtime the moment that text gets rendered.

sections.title: Theming in code
sections.html:
Under the hood, the app starts from Material 2 with an opt-in Material 3 mode that derives a full colour scheme from a single seed. In Material 3 mode, the theme helper resolves all colour roles once and applies them across the view tree, which is also the hook extension themes plug into. Base palettes live in colors_m3.xml alongside its night variant.

In Classic mode, views use fixed colours and extension palettes map onto those slots. Whenever you want a colour change to ripple cleanly across the entire app, make it in the theme helper instead of hunting through individual layouts.

sections.title: Layout variants, and the trap that keeps biting
sections.html:
Core screens ship with multiple layout variants: Classic, Material 3, Sleek, and a Terminal layout for the server screen. Because activities choose their layout dynamically at runtime, adding a new view means either adding it to every layout variant or writing defensive lookups when a variant omits it.

This one bit us in production before: a settings card was added only to the classic layout, which threw a null pointer crash in Material 3 mode, locking users out of the very settings screen where they could switch themes back. Keep this two-line habit everywhere:

View card = findViewById(R.id.card_my_feature);
if (card == null) return;      // this layout variant may not have it
card.setOnClickListener(v -> openMyFeature());

sections.title: Branding and assets
sections.html:
Icons, the K monogram, and brand colours live in branding/ and are generated via script, so updating an asset means editing one source instead of twenty PNGs. Interface typography uses font_koda and logs/code use font_koda_mono, with their license files tracked right alongside all third-party licenses.

Minecraft server jars and Java runtimes are never bundled inside the APK. Downloading and verifying them on demand keeps the install tiny and keeps licensing clean. The app only ships its own assets, bundled server-side helper plugins, and license notices.

sections.title: The design rules
sections.html:
A handful of simple rules keep the app feeling cohesive, and breaking them sticks out immediately once you spend ten minutes using it:

  • Stick to the Koda palette instead of inventing random greys. Orange highlights actions, green signals online health, and red warns of danger.
  • Keep buttons and cards at a 12 dp corner radius on flat surfaces without heavy drop shadows.
  • Ship every new UI string in English, German, Chinese, and Polish.
  • Keep utility sheets focused: clear controls and one clear outcome, not walls of text.
  • When adding a step to an existing flow, match the layout of that flow rather than inventing a second style.

sections.title: Adding a screen or a setting
sections.html:
New screens are plain Android activities paired with XML layouts, wired up directly with findViewById and click listeners. Skipping a heavy navigation framework keeps each screen self-contained and easy to read on its own.

To add a new setting, mirror an existing card in both settings layouts and wire it up in the settings activity, or inject it dynamically the same way extension rows work. To add a new native server tab, extend the tab list and panel handler (extension server tabs do the exact same thing programmatically, so they're a great reference to follow).

sections.title: The database
sections.html:
The control plane runs on Supabase with a deliberately small, easy-to-audit schema. Raw tables stay locked off from direct API access; every action a client is allowed to take goes through an explicit database function.

TableWhat it stores
koda_usersone row per device: app UUID, device token, linked Minecraft account, nickname, permissions, and ban state
koda_serversone row per server: owner, software type, version, port, join address, live state, and join address history
koda_portsthe shared port pool, allocated and freed exclusively by edge functions
releasesapp releases with changelog copy, channel, banner artwork, and publish flag
app_settingsremote flags: maintenance mode, minimum supported versions, and feature toggles
support_tickets, support_ticket_messagessupport tickets and reply threads, plus the encrypted personal chat
extension_*the extension registry: packages, versions, review state, and reports

Naming stays strictly consistent: client-callable RPCs start with rpc_, while internal database helpers start with fn_. Read RPCs stand in for direct table queries, and every write RPC verifies the caller's device token inside the function itself instead of blindly trusting request parameters.

sections.title: Edge functions
sections.html:
Lightweight Deno edge functions handle everything that requires private credentials or server-side authority: allocating and releasing ports, checking server name availability, creating and deleting DNS records, provisioning Java runtimes, and handing out tunnel configs once a device token checks out.

Edge functions are the only layer that holds external service secrets. Incoming requests pass the app UUID and device token, and a single shared helper in supabase/functions/_shared handles caller verification consistently across every endpoint.

sections.title: Inside KodaDash
sections.html:
KodaDash is a compact Java plugin that spins up its own HTTP server using the JDK's built-in server classes, so it carries zero third-party dependencies beyond the Minecraft plugin API. Each area registers its own clean handler: console, players, files, settings, plugins, logs, backups, schedules, stats, efficiency, and server actions.

The console handler is where the cleverness lives: it attaches a Log4j appender via a dynamic proxy, maintains a bounded per-client queue on a dedicated writer thread, and tags every streamed event with a monotonically increasing line index. If your browser disconnects when your phone sleeps, it reconnects and picks up on the exact line it missed.

To avoid race conditions, KodaDash never overwrites files owned by the Android app. The app mirrors stats, backups, and schedules into the server directory, and KodaDash treats them as read-only so every piece of state has a single clear owner.

sections.title: The Discord release bot
sections.html:
A small Node.js service polls the releases table for anything marked published that hasn't been announced yet. It runs server-side with the service role key, posts the changelog and banner image to Discord, and flips the announced flag afterward so restarting the bot never causes duplicate posts.

The bot is strictly an announcer: it never creates or edits releases itself. Publishing stays an explicit button click in the operator admin panel.

sections.title: The website
sections.html:
The website is a fast static app paired with a live dashboard that talks to the same Supabase backend using the public anon key and standard user login. It focuses on the things a phone screen isn't great for: viewing all your servers side by side, reading changelogs comfortably, managing extensions, or checking server status while you're at a desk.

Legal notices and third-party license lists come from the exact same source files bundled in the Android app, so fixing a typo once updates both places. These docs live right in the same site and repository as the code they document.

sections.title: The admin tools
sections.html:
Two private operator tools sit on top of the service role key, which is why neither lives in the public repository:

  • The web admin panel for publishing app releases, uploading release banners, and reviewing extension submissions.
  • The Android admin app for urgent on-the-go operations: user and device bans, support tickets, email tools, DNS management, and server triage.

If you self-host your own KodaHosting instance, you can either build lightweight admin tools of your own or manage rows directly in the Supabase dashboard, which works fine for smaller setups.

sections.title: The security model
sections.html:
Yes, the app ships with a public API key, and that's completely intentional because that key alone can't authorize any mutation. Every write carries the device's UUID and a per-installation device token, and server-side functions verify that exact pair before modifying a single row.

  • Device tokens are randomly generated per installation and rotate automatically whenever a device resets.
  • Row level security stays enabled everywhere, with zero permissive open policies on client tables.
  • Admin functions check an explicit allowlist on top of credentials, so merely possessing a key isn't enough to act as an admin.
  • Anti-tamper checks guard the app's own state and identity, kept intentionally narrow so normal users never hit false positives.
  • Attack simulations live in the repo and continuously test the classic abuse paths using the public key: tokenless writes, privilege escalation, ticket spoofing, and raw table reads. Every one of them has to fail.
Server-side plugins keep their credentials separate too. Your KodaDash token lives inside the server folder rather than the app, and even a leaked dashboard token can never delete backups.

sections.title: API reference
sections.html:

Errors

Failed requests return { "error": "name" } paired with a standard HTTP status code. A 401 means your session expired and you need to sign in again. A 429 includes a retry_after duration in seconds; the web UI pauses cleanly with a countdown until that window clears rather than dumping raw errors on screen.

The extension submission pipeline enforces a few extra invariants: version_code must strictly increase, only one version per extension can sit in review at once, and package SHA-256 hashes are always verified post-upload. The live status page links straight here so real-time metrics and their exact API endpoints stay connected.

sections.title: Working on the code
sections.html:
Development splits across two repositories: a private day-to-day repo and a public mirror. A dedicated mirror script copies tracked source files, filters out local helper scripts, IDE files, and database backups, and scans every file for private instance data before pushing. If an unfamiliar secret-like pattern shows up, the push aborts automatically. That safety net is what makes publishing a codebase this size sustainably possible.

Branching stays lightweight: features happen on short-lived branches, releases get tagged, and the public mirror gets clean snapshot commits. If you fork the project, you can use the exact same publish script to protect your own instance secrets.

sections.title: The checks that run around a change
sections.html:
None of these checks exist just to pad a CI badge. Every single one was added after that exact mistake actually made it onto a phone at least once:
