sections.title: Making a release
sections.html:
Shipping a release means bumping the version, building signed artifacts, creating a row in releases, and uploading a banner. The order matters because the app checks the database for updates rather than relying on the store listing alone.

  1. Increment versionCode and versionName in Gradle, then build a signed app bundle for Google Play and a signed APK for direct downloads.
  2. Insert a draft entry in releases with the changelog, channel, and banner image, keeping it unpublished while you double-check everything.
  3. Flip the published flag: the in-app update prompt starts offering the new build, and the Discord bot announces it automatically.

Anyone running an older build sees your changelog right inside the update screen, so write changelogs for real humans rather than dumping raw git commit messages.

sections.title: Licensing, in plain words
sections.html:
KodaHosting is free software released strictly under the GNU General Public License v3. Source files carry a short header pointing to the full license text. If you fork the code and distribute your build, keep those headers and the GPLv3 terms intact so your users get the exact same freedoms you received.

Third-party libraries and licenses are published in two places on purpose: inside the app under Settings, Licenses, and online at host.kodanetwork.eu/licenses.html so anyone can inspect them before installing. Whenever you add a new dependency, make sure its license lands there too.

Extensions are separate works that talk to KodaHosting over its documented bridge API, so they aren't forced under GPLv3. Every extension picks and declares its own license, which the app surfaces clearly to users. That's why license is required in every manifest and why the store strongly encourages linking source code.

sections.title: When something goes wrong
sections.html:
Most hiccups have a straightforward cause, and the app usually points you right to it before you have to dig:

SymptomWhere to look first
Server starts and immediately stopsopen the console tab; the crash card identifies the cause and usually offers a one-tap fix
Friends can't connectverify the live join address on the dashboard and make sure the server actually shows online
Server dies when the screen turns offcheck Android battery optimization settings; the app needs background exemptions enabled
Downloads keep failingcheck the network alarm and open the verbose app log under Log in the console tab
An update isn't showing upcheck your installed version in Settings and confirm the release is marked published
A newly added plugin breaks startuphead to the plugins tab, toggle off the newest jar, and check the console again

Still stuck? Open the debug log screen and attach everything to a support ticket in one tap. That gives way more context than trying to describe the error from memory.

sections.title: Questions that come up often
sections.html:
Does my server keep running when I close the app?

Yes. Servers run inside an Android foreground service with a persistent notification, and onboarding walks you through battery exemptions so Android doesn't put it to sleep. You can still watch the console and manage everything through KodaDash while the phone screen is off.

Do I have to create an account?

Nope. Hosting works completely without an account. Creating one simply adds the web dashboard, easy recovery on a new phone, and family sharing permissions.

Are my worlds uploaded to the cloud?

Never. Your world files stay locally on your phone unless you explicitly initiate a device-to-device transfer, and even then they travel encrypted straight between your two phones.

Why isn't the app available on the Play Store for every phone or country?

Running a real Minecraft server takes solid RAM and a modern Android WebView. Keeping store eligibility honest prevents people with unsupported devices from running into crashes and frustration.

Can I host more than one server at the same time?

Yes, as long as your phone has the memory for it. The app monitors your combined RAM budget automatically, and you can hibernate worlds you aren't playing so they take zero memory or battery.

Where can I get help?

Open a support ticket right inside the app or drop into the Discord server. And for personal stuff that has nothing to do with Minecraft servers, the encrypted personal chat is always there too.

index.x: KodaHosting turns an Android phone into a real Minecraft server. It's not a game client, and it's not a remote control talking to someone else's cloud box. The server process runs right on your phone, your world files live in your phone's storage, and the app wraps the whole thing in a clean control panel. Once you keep that in mind, pretty much every design decision in this codebase clicks into place, even the slightly unusual ones. Under the hood, the system splits into three parts. Keeping them separate in your head makes troubleshooting a lot easier: The device plane is the Android app itself. It downloads server jars and Java runtimes, starts and stops processes, streams the console, browses and edits files, runs backups, and applies config changes. Whenever something actually mutates your server, it happens here. The connectivity plane is the tunnel. A bundled reverse proxy client forwards your Minecraft ports and web dashboard through a public server, so your friends can join cleanly without you touching router port forwarding or exposing your home IP. The control plane is Supabase. It tracks which devices belong to which account, which servers exist, which ports are allocated, which app releases are live, and which extensions passed review. Every write runs through a server-side function that checks a per-device token. There's also a fourth piece that's easy to overlook at first: KodaDash. It's a Java plugin running inside your Minecraft server that serves a web dashboard on port 7867. The Android app mirrors small JSON snapshots for stats, backups, and schedules into the server folder, and KodaDash reads them. That's how the web dashboard still shows sensible numbers even while your phone's screen is off and sleeping.

The public repository gives you the full source code, but it obviously can't include a live production instance. Keys, accounts, domains, and operator admin tools stay private by design. Here's where the boundary sits: Left out on purpose What it covers secrets_local.h the Supabase URL, public key, AI key, and tunnel host compiled into the native layer The Supabase project database rows, storage buckets, auth users, and edge function secrets Tunnel and DNS credentials the reverse proxy token and DNS provider keys used for custom domains Signing material the release keystore, passwords, and Google Play credentials The admin tools the operator web panel and the Kotlin admin app One detail stays public intentionally: the imprint and privacy policy list a real operator and address. German law requires it, and honestly, a hosted service that hides who runs it isn't worth trusting anyway.

Clone the repository and run an initial build with JDK 21. Create a Supabase project and apply the SQL files inside supabase/ in order: first migrations/, then security_fix_*.sql, and finally the remaining feature SQL (releases, extensions, notifications, KodaDash beta, and profile avatar). Each script reloads the API schema automatically. Set up the storage buckets: make artifacts, release_images, support_attachments, extension_assets, and avatars public, and keep extension_packages and data_exports private. Deploy the edge functions and configure their secrets. supabase/README.md documents the complete list. Don't skip get-tunnel-config, because the app calls it to pull its tunnel credentials. Run an frps server (vps-https/frps.toml.example gives you a hardened baseline) and drop its address along with your Supabase URL and public key into the native header file. Build a signed release APK and install it. On first launch, the app registers the device and creates the database row everything else attaches to. Optional: wire up the Discord release bot with your own bot token. The team admin panel and Android admin app aren't included in the public repo. A brand-new instance starts empty on purpose. The app will still launch without a backend, but first-run device registration won't succeed and most cloud-backed screens will stay quiet.

The project is a single Gradle module paired with a small native layer that boots the embedded JVM. The first compile takes a few minutes while dependencies settle; incremental builds after that are fast. export JAVA_HOME=/path/to/jdk-21 # newer JDKs break the Gradle version in use./gradlew:app:assembleDebug # debug apk./gradlew:app:assembleRelease -PKEYSTORE_PW=... -PKEY_PW=... adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk./gradlew:app:testDebugUnitTest # unit tests, finishes in seconds Watch out for signature mismatches: debug and release builds use different signing keys, so Android won't let you install one directly over the other. Pick which build type lives on your test phone early, or you'll have to uninstall and wipe local server data to switch. Watch out for silent logs in release: release builds strip out all Android log calls, both in app code and framework wrappers. Logcat stays completely quiet in release mode, so never rely on it to debug a release APK. Surface diagnostics in the UI instead, or use the app's built-in debug log screen. Target hardware is arm64 running Android 11 or newer. The APK only ships arm64 native libraries, so an x86 emulator won't be able to run servers.

The app keeps its navigation flat: one home screen, one main server screen, and a focused set of setup flows and utility sheets around them. Here's the quick map: Screen What you do there Main see all your servers as cards, check live resource totals, and jump into settings, support, or these docs Create server walk through name, software type, Minecraft version, RAM, world setup, join address, and optional modpack Server detail five tabs per server: dashboard, console, files, mods and plugins, and settings Settings appearance, account, support, legal docs, developer options, and the extension hub Extensions install, toggle, update, and configure app extensions Themes switch built-in colour schemes or apply themes provided by extensions Support open support tickets, file bug reports, or use the encrypted personal chat Onboarding first-launch setup: language, terms, optional account, background battery permissions, and nickname

Your home screen shows every server as a card with its name, server software, Minecraft version, and live status. Tap a card to open the full server screen, or long-press it for quick actions without leaving the list. Each card also puts the numbers you actually care about up front: player count, RAM usage, and uptime. Hibernated servers appear dimmed with a one-tap wake button. When a server is mid-startup or shutting down, the button turns into an animated status indicator so you know it's working without having to open the console. At the top of the screen, you'll find shortcuts to settings, support, Discord, the debug log, and the button to spin up a new server. Right above the list, a summary card adds up how many servers you have, how many are currently online, and how much memory they're using combined.

The creation wizard walks you through one choice at a time in a fixed order, because choices like software type and version affect everything that comes after. You'll set the name and join address first, then pick your server software, Minecraft version, memory budget, and world configuration. Server type: Paper, Purpur, Folia, and Vanilla if you want plugins or vanilla gameplay; Fabric, Forge, and NeoForge for mods; or PumpkinMC, a native server that runs without Java at all. Minecraft version: filtered to versions that your chosen server software actually ships, complete with quick notes on plugin and mod compatibility. Memory: the slider shows what your phone can safely spare alongside any other running servers. World: configure world type, custom seed, or quick presets like a flat world for testing builds. Setup mode: pick the Koda design to start with a tuned config and solid gameplay defaults, or choose a completely clean vanilla setup. Once you finish the wizard, the app creates the server locally and registers it in the cloud. On its very first start, it automatically downloads the server jar and the matching Java runtime if needed, showing live progress right inside the console.

When you tap into a server, you land on the dashboard tab. It's built to answer three questions in two seconds: is everything healthy, who's playing right now, and what actions do I need? Status and connectivity sit right at the top, with a copyable join address and a button to customize it. Below that, the player roster shows everyone online with their skins; tapping any player opens their full sheet with stats, live inventory, and moderation controls. CPU and RAM meters update in real time, and the quick-action bar lets you start, stop, or restart the server, automatically counting down in chat first if players are connected. If your server ever crashes, the dashboard swaps in a crash card with a classified root cause, a concrete suggested fix, and the final lines of the log. Applying a suggested fix takes one tap and never makes blind guesses: it adjusts one specific known setting and tells you exactly what it changed.

The console streams raw server output live, strips out messy Minecraft ANSI colour codes, and highlights log levels so warnings and errors jump off the screen. Auto-scroll follows incoming lines until you scroll up to read something, then stays pinned right where you left it so you can actually read a stack trace in peace. Just above the command bar sits a row of quick-command chips, and extensions can append their own chips there too. Anything you type goes straight to the server's stdin, so vanilla commands and plugin commands both work exactly as expected. Copy puts the visible console buffer on your clipboard, ready to paste into a support ticket. Log opens the app's own verbose log, which is where you look if a runtime download or tunnel startup fails before Minecraft even boots. AI crash analysis can walk through a crash log with you, and always asks for explicit consent before sending a single line off your phone.

The files tab gives you a full file manager rooted at your server directory. Tap folders to navigate, tap text files to open the built-in editor, or long-press any item to rename, copy, cut, delete, or share it. Import pulls files in from anywhere Android's file picker can see, including local storage, other apps, and cloud drives. Unpack here extracts ZIP and RAR archives right in place. If a RAR archive is password-protected, the app tells you plainly instead of failing silently. Export zips the entire server directory into your Downloads folder without an extra wrapper folder, so you can re-import it directly later. NBT viewer lets you inspect binary NBT files like player data and level.dat as a clean, readable tree (read-only on purpose so nothing gets corrupted). The built-in text editor handles files up to 1 MB with clean formatting for properties, JSON, and YAML. If you hit save while the server is still online, it reminds you that many config files are only read at startup.

Mods and plugins live in their own tab, complete with a built-in Modrinth browser. You can search, filter automatically by your server's software and Minecraft version, install with a tap, and update with a tap. Your installed list pulls metadata directly out of each jar (name, version, authors, and icon) and falls back to Modrinth when a jar doesn't bundle its own icon. Flipping a toggle disables a jar cleanly by renaming it rather than deleting it, and removing a jar moves it to trash for a while first in case you change your mind. Don't mix up server jars and app extensions. This tab manages plugins and mods running inside Minecraft. App extensions customize the KodaHosting app itself and are covered later in these docs.

Starting a server looks like a single tap, but a lot happens behind the curtain: the app checks your phone's free RAM and network budget, gets the right runtime ready, writes any generated config files, launches the process, and watches the console for the startup completion line before flipping the status to online. Stopping always tries the graceful route first. It tells the server to save the world and shut down cleanly, and only terminates the process if it stops responding. A force-kill option is available when a server is truly hung, tucked behind a confirmation dialog because killing a JVM mid-write can corrupt chunks. Restarts go through the exact same graceful stop sequence so nobody loses inventory or builds. If players are online when you trigger a restart, the app broadcasts a countdown warning in chat first.

You can change a server's Minecraft version from the dashboard settings wheel. Because shifting versions touches world formats and plugin compatibility, the app treats it as a real migration rather than a casual toggle. Only versions officially published for your current server software appear in the list. Upgrades strongly recommend taking a backup first, though you can choose to skip it. Downgrades require a backup before continuing, since Minecraft worlds and chunks aren't backwards-compatible. Your previous server jar stays safely in place until the new version boots cleanly. Plugins and mods won't auto-migrate across major Minecraft updates. Once the switch finishes, the app nudges you to check the mods/plugins tab, where Modrinth update checks usually locate matching builds right away.

Backups are standard ZIP snapshots of your entire server folder stored alongside the app, and they're the fastest way to make sure a bad plugin or accidental TNT mishap stays a minor inconvenience. You can trigger a backup manually whenever you want, or set up automatic backups on stop, daily, or both. Keep count sets how many backups to retain before older snapshots rotate out. Restore rolls your server folder back to the selected archive while keeping your current files safe until the restore finishes cleanly. Size and age appear on every backup entry so freeing up storage is an informed choice rather than guesswork. You can only restore a backup while the server is stopped. The app enforces that strictly, and it has saved plenty of worlds from half-written corruption.

The automation sheet lets you schedule recurring chores: restart, stop, save the world, broadcast a chat announcement, or run any console command. Tasks can repeat on an interval or run daily at a specific clock time, and you can optionally tell a task to wait until the server is empty. Most hosts start with a nightly restart paired with a chat warning a few minutes beforehand. When an empty-only restart is queued, the app announces it in chat so nobody gets caught off guard. Everything you configure here is mirrored into the server folder so KodaDash displays the exact same schedule list in the browser.

Player management covers both sides of your community: who's connected right now and everyone who has joined in the past. Tap any player to pull up their skin, total playtime, gameplay stats, and a live inventory view read directly from their save data. Live actions: kick, ban, pardon, op/deop, private message, gamemode switch, teleport, and XP adjustments. Care actions: heal, feed, saturate, plus a full inventory wipe guarded by a double confirmation. Inventory editing: drag items straight between slots to rearrange a player's inventory, written right back into their player data. Whitelist: toggle server-wide whitelist enforcement and add or remove individual players using the server's native whitelist rules.

Your MOTD is the two-line banner players see in their Minecraft multiplayer list, and writing colour codes by hand is nobody's idea of fun. The built-in editor gives you formatting buttons for colours, bold, italic, underline, obfuscated text, resets, and hex colours in all three formats Minecraft accepts. Each toolbar button drops the right code at your cursor without losing your typing position, while a live preview shows how it will look in-game. If you'd rather edit the raw text directly, the plain server.properties view is still right there in the files tab. Tip: drag the bottom edge of the MOTD input box to resize it when you're crafting longer messages on a smaller screen.

You don't need an external file host to serve a custom resource pack. Pick a ZIP from your phone, and the app handles every step: copies it into the server folder, calculates its SHA-1 checksum, updates the pack URL and hash in server.properties, and lets you flip the required-pack toggle on or off. KodaDash serves the pack straight over your tunnel on your server's join address, so players download it automatically on connect. The dashboard shows whether a resource pack is active and how big the download is.

World type, seed, gamemode, difficulty, view and simulation distance, spawn protection, and hardcore mode all live in the settings tab and write directly to server.properties. After saving, the app reads the file back and compares values so any manual edits you made in the text editor never get silently clobbered. If you tweak server.properties by hand while the server is offline, the app spots the mismatch next time you open settings and asks which version you want to keep. That way the UI and the config file never drift out of sync.

Every server gets its own JVM heap limit, and the app keeps an eye on the global ceiling. Android always needs breathing room for itself, so if you launch a second server, the RAM slider automatically caps itself to what's actually free and warns you before pushing the phone into heavy swapping. Because heap size is passed as a JVM launch flag, changing it takes effect on the next restart. The app also feeds your device's real memory budget into crash diagnostics, so if a server runs out of memory, the recommended fix suggests a realistic number for your specific phone rather than a generic guess.

Different Minecraft versions require different Java versions, and bundling all of them inside the APK would make it massive. Instead, KodaHosting downloads the exact runtime a server needs on demand (covering everything from JDK 25 down to Java 17 and Java 8) and remembers that preference per server. Automatic picks the right JDK for your server software and Minecraft version. Manual lets you pin a specific runtime, which is handy if a legacy mod refuses to run on anything newer than Java 17. Fallback keeps your server bootable if a selected runtime is broken, clearly telling you which fallback it used and why. Runtime downloads stream their progress into the console tab. Downloaded runtimes are shared across all servers on your phone, so spinning up a second server on the same Java version is much faster.

Hibernation puts a server to sleep without deleting your work. The app stops the process, releases the join address on the tunnel, packs up the server folder, and leaves a clean marker so your home screen shows a sleeping server instead of a missing one. When you're ready to play again, waking it unpacks the folder, grabs a fresh join address, and boots the server right back up. A hibernated server consumes zero RAM, zero battery, and zero tunnel bandwidth, which makes a big difference if you juggle several worlds on one phone. Device-to-device server transfers use the exact same archive format under the hood, which is why both features share the same packing pipeline.

Running plugins that expect a real database? KodaHosting can run MariaDB or Redis right alongside your Minecraft server on the same phone, using credentials you pick in the setup wizard. Both run as native binaries from the same runtime stack, so there's nothing extra to install. The database card displays everything your plugin config needs (port, username, and generated password), and the data directory sits right beside the server files so normal backups capture both together. If you see the Database server type on the main list, that's simply a standalone MariaDB or Redis instance running without a Minecraft server attached.

Most phones sit behind carrier NAT or a home router where outside players can't connect directly. To solve that, KodaHosting bundles a reverse proxy client that forwards your Minecraft ports and web dashboard through a public relay server. Players connect using the join address shown on your dashboard, which follows the tunnel rather than your home IP. Tunnel credentials aren't baked into the APK. Instead, the app requests them from the backend on demand, caches them for a few hours, and refreshes them quietly in the background. If a tunnel token expires, it heals itself automatically without you ever having to reinstall the app. Join address is assigned automatically when you create a server, and you can change it once per day. Java and Bedrock ports both forward automatically whenever Bedrock crossplay is enabled. KodaDash rides through the same tunnel on its own reserved port band.

If you already own a domain, the custom domain wizard walks you through pointing it at your server with an SRV record. It hands you the exact record values, lets you copy them with one tap, and checks public DNS until the record propagates. You don't need to be a DNS expert; the wizard explains what each record does along the way. Since DNS propagation can take a little while, you can close the wizard and come back later. Your default join address keeps working in the meantime, and you can unlink your custom domain from the same card whenever you want to switch back.

Every server gets two paired ports managed automatically by the app: the local port Minecraft binds to on the phone, and the public port exposed through the tunnel. KodaDash always uses a separate reserved port range so it never bumps into a game server. You can inspect every active and free port right from the dashboard. If another app on your phone is already holding a port, startup stops with a clear explanation and a suggested fix instead of throwing a cryptic crash.

index.h: Network budgets and the network alarm
index.x: Hosting on a phone usually means sharing Wi-Fi or mobile data with everyone else in the house. KodaHosting tracks per-server bandwidth in real time and lets you put sensible guardrails around it. Budget rules cap transfer speeds and split bandwidth across servers so one busy world doesn't choke the rest. The network alarm alerts you when the shared tunnel relay starts getting heavy load, ideally before players feel any lag. Protection mode steps in to stop servers when the network is genuinely overloaded and explains why, rather than letting everyone rubber-band.

KodaDash is a lightweight Java plugin bundled inside your Minecraft server that exposes a web interface over the tunnel. It solves a super practical problem: managing your server from a laptop or browser when you don't have your phone in your hand. Tab What you get Overview live status, online players, RAM usage, TPS history, and info about the phone hosting the server Console live streaming console with scrollback history and log-level filtering Players player list with live inventories, stats, and moderation tools Files browse and edit server files right in your browser Plugins view installed jars, toggle them on or off, and search Modrinth Settings edit server.properties while preserving existing comments KodaDash uses its own access token and optional password. One deliberate safety choice: the backups tab is strictly read-only, so even if someone ever leaked a dashboard token, they couldn't wipe out your only world backups.

Starting with KodaDash 1.2.0, your server exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. Any AI client that speaks remote MCP can inspect server status, read logs and config files, run console commands, and tweak settings without you needing the phone app open. It connects directly to standard MCP clients rather than locking you into an in-app chat box.

A running Paper or Purpur server with KodaDash enabled. KodaHosting v0.147beta / version code 8527 or newer (that build bundles the KodaDash 1.1.0 jar and newer updates). Your HTTPS dashboard URL, such as https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/. Your MCP endpoint is simply that same host with /mcp added.

In KodaDash, head to Settings, AI access (MCP). Inside the Android app, open your server and go to KodaDash, AI access (MCP). Open Connection and switch on Enable MCP. KodaDash generates a dedicated MCP token for you. Copy both the endpoint URL and the token. Your endpoint looks like https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp. Your MCP token is completely separate from your KodaDash login token and your KodaHosting account password. It only grants access to this single server and only to the specific tool groups you switch on. You'll also find built-in How to set up and Troubleshooting rows right inside the app's MCP sheet, so you can grab these steps offline without opening the docs.

Every MCP client asks for the same three ingredients: the endpoint URL, your Bearer token, and the HTTP transport. Only the config file path and key names vary. The table below gives you the quick cheat sheet, followed by copy-paste examples. Even faster: tap Copy JSON in the app's Connection sheet to copy a ready-to-paste mcpServers block. Client Config location Fields to set ZCode MCP server list, New MCP server Type HTTP, URL, Headers JSON Codex ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.…], url, bearer_token_env_var Antigravity ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json serverUrl, headers Claude Code.mcp.json or claude mcp add-json type: http, url, headers Cursor ~/.cursor/mcp.json or.cursor/mcp.json url, headers VS Code.vscode/mcp.json or user mcp.json servers, type: http, url, headers Windsurf ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json serverUrl, headers Claude Desktop Connectors or a stdio bridge OAuth, or mcp-remote for a static Bearer header

Open the MCP server list and pick New MCP server. Name: kodahosting-your-server. Scope: This computer or User. Type: HTTP. Timeout MS: 30000. Protocol version: Auto. URL: https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp. Headers: {"Authorization": "Bearer <mcp-token>"} in either the Form or JSON tab. Save. Your KodaDash tools should pop up in the client's tool list right away. 30000 ms works well for most phones; bump it to 60000 if your device takes a bit longer to wake up. Leave Protocol version on Auto.

[mcp_servers.kodahosting] url = "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp" bearer_token_env_var = "KODA_MCP_TOKEN" Set the token in the shell environment where you launch Codex rather than putting it straight into the TOML file: export KODA_MCP_TOKEN=<mcp-token>. You can also register it via CLI with codex mcp add kodahosting --url https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp --bearer-token-env-var KODA_MCP_TOKEN. If you really need a static header in the file, use [mcp_servers.kodahosting.http_headers] with Authorization = "Bearer...", though the environment variable is much safer.

{ "mcpServers": { "kodahosting": { "serverUrl": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <mcp-token>" } } } } Note that Antigravity expects serverUrl rather than url. Put this in ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json globally, or.agents/mcp_config.json inside a workspace. Via CLI: agy mcp add --type http --header "Authorization: Bearer <mcp-token>" kodahosting https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp.

{ "mcpServers": { "kodahosting": { "type": "http", "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } Save this to.mcp.json or pass it to claude mcp add-json kodahosting '{...}'. Keep in mind Claude Code reads exported shell environment variables and does not automatically load a plain.env file.

{ "mcpServers": { "kodahosting": { "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } Works in either your global ~/.cursor/mcp.json or a project-level.cursor/mcp.json. Cursor automatically picks up Streamable HTTP from the url field.

{ "inputs": [ { "type": "promptString", "id": "koda-mcp-token", "description": "KodaHosting MCP token", "password": true } ], "servers": { "kodahosting": { "type": "http", "url": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:koda-mcp-token}" } } } } Heads up: VS Code uses servers at the top level instead of mcpServers. Drop this into.vscode/mcp.json or open your user config via MCP: Open User Configuration in the Command Palette.

{ "mcpServers": { "kodahosting": { "serverUrl": "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:KODA_MCP_TOKEN}" } } } } Windsurf specifically looks for serverUrl; pasting a snippet with url can fail silently. Hit refresh in the MCP panel after saving.

Claude Desktop's built-in custom connector mainly targets public or OAuth servers, and not every build exposes custom request headers. If your version lets you enter a header, use that. Otherwise, bridge it locally over stdio with mcp-remote: { "mcpServers": { "kodahosting": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp", "--header", "Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER}"], "env": { "AUTH_HEADER": "Bearer <mcp-token>" } } } } If you're on Windows, keep the space inside AUTH_HEADER and pass Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER} so the argument doesn't get split on whitespace. Note that mcp-remote is an external tool and isn't bundled with KodaDash.

Start with the standard mcpServers layout using url and headers. If your client asks for a transport type, select HTTP or Streamable HTTP. If it expects serverUrl instead of url, swap the key name. If it only speaks stdio, put an HTTP-to-stdio bridge in front.

curl -s https://your-server.kodaserv.eu/mcp \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <mcp-token>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' If everything is wired up right, you'll get back a JSON response with a tools array. Seeing a 405 on GET /mcp is completely expected: the endpoint accepts POST requests only and doesn't run an SSE stream.

Area Available tools Read server status, MCP status, console tail, online players, playtime, stats history, files, logs, plugins, server.properties, schedules, and the backup index Console run commands as the console sender (excluding start, stop, restart, and hibernate) Files list, read, write, rename, create directories, and delete. Files up to 16 MB go through files_push in one request; larger jars are assembled in ≤16 MB base64 chunks with files_chunk_append onto a.part name and swapped onto their final path with files_replace_atomic, so a failed transfer never leaves a half-written jar behind Server read and edit server.properties, plus validated single-setting helpers for MOTD, max players, difficulty, gamemode, PvP, whitelist, online-mode, view distance, simulation distance, and spawn protection Plugins list, enable, disable, install from a public HTTPS URL, search Modrinth, and install compatible Modrinth versions with SHA-512 verification An AI client can never start, stop, restart, or hibernate your server. Power controls stay strictly in human hands inside the app or dashboard, and KodaDash rejects those commands even if an AI tries sending them through the console. Dedicated helper tools include mcp_status, modrinth_search, modrinth_install, server_setting, and the big-file helpers files_push, files_chunk_append, and files_replace_atomic. The tools/list call always reflects the exact tool set of the installed KodaDash version, so newer plugins can add tools without a config change on your side.

Read-only mode hides every write tool completely. Great when you just want an AI to diagnose a lag spike or inspect logs. Capability switches let you independently toggle console commands, file writes, server.properties edits, plugin actions, and Modrinth downloads. Regenerate invalidates your current MCP token on the spot and issues a fresh one. Just remember to update your AI client config afterward. Destructive actions (and overwriting existing files) require an explicit confirm:true flag. Modrinth installs always check the SHA-512 hash against version metadata and delete the file immediately on mismatch. Modrinth lookups and downloads are locked strictly to api.modrinth.com and cdn.modrinth.com over HTTPS; private, loopback, and reserved IP ranges are blocked. Every single tool call gets logged to plugins/KodaDash/mcp-audit.log, with file contents and any argument names containing password, secret, or token automatically redacted. plugins/KodaDash/config.yml, the audit log itself, and.frpc.toml are completely off-limits to MCP file tools. Treat your MCP token like a root password. Anyone holding it can invoke whichever tools you've enabled, so keep it out of public repos and screenshots.

When a client connects, KodaDash sends an initial system prompt giving the AI practical context: KodaHosting environment details, server software and version, loaded worlds, plugins, live players and TPS, plus your phone's model, Android version, RAM, battery, and free storage. It also reinforces the ground rules: never start or stop the server, ask before destructive changes, never expose tokens, and prefer read-only checks. Software and version data reported by the running server are treated as authoritative. The app/cloud mirror in server-info.json is explicitly tagged as secondary and potentially stale, so an outdated cloud server_version is never mistaken for reality. Even if an AI client drops the initial prompt later, it can pull the exact same snapshot anytime with the read-only server_context tool.

Symptom What to check 404 Either MCP or KodaDash is turned off. Both need to be enabled for the endpoint to exist. 401 Your token is mistyped or was rotated. Copy the active token from Connection. 405 on GET Expected behavior. Send POST requests; SSE isn't used here. No connection Make sure the server is online and your HTTPS dashboard loads normally at https://<server>/. Tools are missing Read-only mode or a specific capability switch is turned off under Permissions. Old plugin KodaDash updates when the app launches the server. Update to build 8527 or newer and restart the server once. If an AI ever does something surprising, open plugins/KodaDash/mcp-audit.log first. It records the exact tool called, redacted arguments, outcome, and duration for every request.

Want friends on consoles, tablets, or phones to join your Java world? Turning on Bedrock crossplay installs Geyser and Floodgate, generates configs pre-matched to your server setup, and forwards the extra UDP port Bedrock expects. If you're running PumpkinMC, Bedrock support is native to the server itself, so it's just a built-in toggle. Either way, your dashboard displays both join details cleanly: the Java address and the Bedrock address with its port.

Enabling Simple Voice Chat installs the right plugin or mod for your server software, opens the extra UDP port over the tunnel, and writes out the voice chat config with the proper public port and address. Both Java and Bedrock players get working proximity voice without you having to rent a separate server.

You don't need an account to host servers on KodaHosting. Creating one is completely optional, and it unlocks the web dashboard, server recovery when you switch phones, and family sharing permissions. You can sign in with email and password or with Google. Notice the direction of trust: your account links to your device, not the other way around. Your local device token remains the credential that authorizes writes, and it never leaves your phone.

Linking proves a Minecraft username belongs to you, which powers the lobby and the /join command. The app gives you a short verification code; hop into the lobby server, run /link with that code, and your Minecraft profile appears right on your account card. One Minecraft account can only be linked to one device at a time. If you move it to a new phone, the old device loses the link deliberately so shared setups don't drift out of sync.

Your nickname is what other players see in the public server list and lobby instead of an internal device ID. The app asks you to pick one after first launch (and gently reminds you at most once a day when opening social screens), and you can update it anytime in settings.

index.t: Moving servers to a new device
index.h: Moving servers to a new device
index.x: Upgrading your phone doesn't mean starting your worlds over. Device transfer moves an entire server directly from one phone to another over your local Wi-Fi, encrypted end to end. The old phone packs and serves the archive, the new phone pulls it down and adopts it, and your join addresses come along for the ride. Pairing works either by picking the nearby device or entering an 8-character code, and the receiving phone always shows a confirmation prompt naming the sender. Encryption uses an ephemeral key that only exists for that transfer window, keeping your world files unreadable even on a shared network. Safe cleanup only runs after the receiving phone confirms everything arrived intact. If your Wi-Fi drops halfway through, your original copy is untouched.

One main account can own several servers while letting friends or family help run them with granular permissions. You decide per person who can start, stop, hibernate, delete, manage players, install plugins, or send console commands, all controlled with simple switches while the main account stays in full control. Because everyone signs in with their own account, permissions follow the person rather than a specific phone. Need to revoke access? Flip a single switch and it takes effect on their very next action.

Got a spare Android phone sitting in a drawer? Connect two phones with a USB cable to turn them into a mini hosting cluster. One phone acts as the master controller, showing a unified dashboard for both devices and starting or stopping servers on the secondary phone. They talk over a tiny JSON protocol straight across USB, so it doesn't even depend on Wi-Fi. Set the secondary phone to USB file transfer mode. The USB accessory filter is already built into the app manifest, so the cluster links up automatically without manual pairing.

You can reach support without leaving the app: write a subject and message, attach screenshots or logs if they help, and follow the full reply thread in one place. Bug reports and server reports feed into the exact same ticket system with a quicker form, so nothing slips through the cracks. Opening a ticket requires an account so replies actually have somewhere to go. Your ticket list tracks the live status of every thread and keeps the full conversation history.

Alongside regular support tickets, there's a direct, end-to-end encrypted chat with the developer. Your phone generates the keys locally, the private key never leaves your device, and every message is encrypted with ECDH and AES-GCM before it's ever stored. On the other end, only the developer can decrypt messages using a key stored behind a PIN in a separate admin app. The whole idea is simple: honest conversations stay strictly between two people, and nobody in the middle, not even the database storing the ciphertext, can read them.

If something during a session signals that someone might be going through a really hard time, the app shows a calm, quiet screen with one goal: reminding you that someone cares and offering real ways to reach out, including crisis hotlines, youth chat support, and the personal chat. It never blocks your access, never reports anything anywhere, and never touches your servers. Dismissing it only has a brief pause so it doesn't get tapped away by accident. It's in the app simply because the people using this software are real people, and the person building it is too.

Bans are always a last resort, and the app treats them that way. Server names get checked up front, abuse reports are reviewed by a real human, and if a server does get banned, the screen clearly explains why and lets you download a backup of your world instead of stranding your data. Device bans only exist for persistent abuse that tries to survive reinstalls. They're rare, and the checks behind them are deliberately narrow: tampering with the app's own protected state or forging device identities, and nothing else.

Extensions let anyone add new screens, translations, themes, settings entries, and server tabs to KodaHosting without forking the app or waiting on an official update. Each extension is just a ZIP file containing a manifest and, if it has a UI, a lightweight web view. Zero native code is ever loaded dynamically, which keeps the app compliant with Play Store rules and ensures a buggy extension can't crash the app around it. The quickest way to learn is to peek at the working examples right in the repository: Koda Lab, an interactive test bench that exercises every bridge call and prints raw responses Live Log, a clean custom screen in roughly a hundred lines Polski, a real production language pack Ocean, a custom colour theme combined with UI tweaks The written reference, along with the full JSON schema right beside it

my-extension.kodaext (a ZIP, files at the root) manifest.json required ui/index.html required when the extension has a screen ui/app.js, ui/style.css your interface lang/es.json language packs you contribute automations.json automation rules icon.png 128x128, shown in the hub Here's a kitchen-sink manifest that touches almost every feature. Treat it like a menu and strip out whatever your extension doesn't need: { "schema": 1, "id": "eu.example.mypack", "name": "My Pack", "version": "1.0.0", "versionCode": 1, "author": "Your name", "description": "What it does, in one sentence.", "license": "GPL-3.0-or-later", "source_url": "https://github.com/you/mypack", "minAppVersion": 8514, "permissions": ["servers.read", "console.read", "storage", "http:discord.com"], "ui": { "entry": "ui/index.html", "title": "My Pack" }, "contributes": { "languages": [ { "code": "es", "name": "Espanol", "file": "lang/es.json" } ], "themes": [ { "id": "ocean", "name": "Ocean", "color": "#006874" } ], "settings": [ { "title": "My Pack", "subtitle": "Open the panel", "target": "overview" } ], "server_tabs": [ { "id": "panel", "title": "Panel", "target": "server" } ], "ui": { "hide": ["btn_github_main"], "console_chips": ["/tps", "time set day"] } }, "automations": "automations.json" } Field Rule schema must be 1 id lowercase reverse-domain identifier, at least two dot-separated segments, max 64 characters name max 48 characters, displayed in the extension hub version and versionCode versionCode must strictly increase with every update license required; shown right beside the extension in the app source_url recommended; displayed as a clickable source link minAppVersion minimum KodaHosting build number required to install permissions capabilities your code needs, enforced by the bridge contributes languages, themes, settings rows, server tabs, and UI tweaks added to the app

Every extension screen runs inside a sandboxed WebView that can only access its own package files. To interact with KodaHosting, your page calls a single global object, window.koda, which the app injects before your scripts execute. Every method returns a Promise resolving to a plain JSON object, and errors come back as an object with an error property instead of throwing unhandled exceptions. const { servers } = await koda.servers.list(); const first = servers[0]; const { lines } = await koda.console.tail(first.id, 200); await koda.storage.set('lastServer', first.id); const saved = await koda.storage.get('lastServer'); // { value: '...' } const theme = await koda.theme(); // colours, so your page can match the app const { lang } = await koda.locale(); koda.ui.toast('Hello from my pack'); const { ok } = await koda.ui.confirm('Restart?', 'Players will be kicked.'); Call What it returns koda.api, koda.version bridge version info so you can gracefully handle older app builds koda.servers.list(), get(id) servers with a stable schema: id, name, type, mcVersion, state, port, address, ramMB, maxPlayers koda.console.tail(id, lines) recent console lines, up to 1,000 lines koda.storage.get/set/remove/keys private key-value storage scoped to your extension (1 MB limit) koda.ui.toast, koda.ui.confirm native toast and confirmation dialog styled to match the app koda.theme(), koda.locale() active app palette and language code so your UI blends right in

Declare everything you need in manifest.json. The app enforces permissions at runtime, so calling koda.servers.list() without servers.read simply returns an error object. Permission Current status storage, servers.read, console.read live today console.send, servers.control declared, next phase (gated by in-app confirmation) players.read, players.actions, files.read, notifications declared, next phase http:host scoped outbound HTTP access for one specific domain Only read permissions and storage are active right now. Install Koda Lab on your device to inspect the exact live payload every bridge call returns on your build, rather than guessing.

// lang/es.json, the keys are the app's string resource names { "tab_dashboard": "Panel", "jars_title": "MODS Y PLUGINS", "sd_toast_log_copied": "Registro copiado", "ext_ui_chips_count": "%1$d comandos extra en la consola." } Language packs don't have to translate every single string in the app. Anything you omit falls back cleanly to the user's current language, so even a partial pack is immediately useful and easy to expand over time. Just be careful with format placeholders like %1$s or %1$d: keep them verbatim, because a missing or extra placeholder will crash Android when that string formats. python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py path/to/lang/es.json Run that checker before shipping. It validates every key against the app's actual string resources and flags typos that would otherwise sit silently unused. Users apply a language pack from the extension's action sheet (requiring a quick restart), and disabling the extension automatically restores their previous language.

"themes": [ { "id": "ocean", "name": "Ocean", "color": "#006874" }, { "id": "midnight", "name": "Midnight", "color": "#00D9FF", "colors": { "primary": "#00D9FF", "surface": "#07070F", "card": "#14141F", "text": "#EDEDF5", "text_dim": "#8C8C9C", "error": "#FF4455" } } ] Supplying just color gives the app a seed colour to feed into its Material 3 engine, generating a harmonious palette across buttons, cards, and highlights automatically. If you want total visual control, add a colors object with any combination of primary, surface, card, text, text_dim, outline, online, and error. The app overrides the generated roles with yours and computes readable contrast colours for text on top of your accents. Contributed themes show up in two places on purpose: inside the extension's action sheet and in Settings, Appearance, Themes. Each theme gets its own toggle, and enabling one automatically switches off whichever theme was active before. App theme mode How your theme applies Material 3 mode restyles the entire UI by resolving colour roles across the view tree Classic design maps your accent, surfaces, cards, text, and outlines onto the classic palette slots

"settings": [ { "title": "My Pack", "subtitle": "Everything in one screen", "target": "overview" } ] Settings entries appear right beneath the extension hub inside the app's Settings screen. Each row automatically gets a small info icon displaying the extension name, version, author, and license so users always know what's built-in and what comes from an extension. Tapping a row opens your UI with #target appended to the URL, making it easy to deep-link straight to a specific sub-view. Each extension can contribute up to four settings rows.

"server_tabs": [ { "id": "panel", "title": "Panel", "target": "server" } ] This adds your own custom tab to every server's detail screen. When opened, the app passes the active server ID in the URL hash, like #server&server=the-server-id, so your page knows exactly which server the user is looking at. Grabbing it takes two lines of JavaScript: const parts = location.hash.replace('#', '').split('&'); const server = (parts.find(p => p.startsWith('server=')) || '').split('=')[1]; One honest caveat: the optional sleek layout doesn't have a shared tab container, so contributed server tabs are skipped there. Extensions can add up to four server tabs each.

"ui": { "hide": ["btn_github_main"], "console_chips": ["/tps", "/list", "time set day"] } hide removes specific UI elements by their Android view IDs, while console_chips adds custom quick-command buttons right above the server console input. Both take effect automatically whenever the extension is enabled, without any extra toggles to dig for.

{ "schema": 1, "automations": [ { "id": "crash-watch", "name": "Crash warning", "when": { "type": "log_match", "server": "*", "pattern": "(?i)(crash|exception)" }, "then": [ { "type": "notify", "title": "Crash on {server}", "text": "{line}" }, { "type": "http", "method": "POST", "url": "https://discord.com/api/webhooks/...", "body": { "content": "{line}" } } ] } ] } Automation rules pair a trigger (server state changes, regex log matches, or schedules) with a list of actions (notifications, webhooks, or console commands). Template variables like {server} and {line} expand automatically when a rule fires. The schema is finalized and validated at install time today, while the background rule runner lands in the next phase. You can already ship valid automations.json definitions in your packages now.

# validate the manifest and build the package python3 extensions/tools/pack_extension.py extensions/examples/koda-lab # check a language pack before you ship it python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py my/pack/lang/es.json Both scripts enforce the exact same validation checks the Android app runs. Catching an unknown view ID, missing translation file, malformed hex colour, or stagnant version code on your laptop is a lot nicer than hitting it on someone's phone. To test locally, sideload your package via Settings, Extensions, + and pick the file. Updating an extension preserves its saved storage; uninstalling clears storage cleanly. You'll also find a Reload action in the hub menu so you can iterate without reinstalling every time.

The extension store lives at host.kodanetwork.eu/store and mirrors straight into the app's extension hub under Discover. You publish on the website, users install inside the app, and both sides speak to the same public API.

Sign in with your KodaHosting account, pick your.kodaext archive, enter the name, version, license, and source URL, and hit submit. Your browser computes the SHA-256 hash and the backend verifies it after upload, inspecting the manifest inside the archive and rejecting anything with an invalid ID, version code, license, or permission set. Every submission goes through human review first, and the first approved release puts your extension live in the catalog. Every submission sits in one of five clear states: PENDING while waiting for review, APPROVED once live, REJECTED with a written reason, DELISTED if pulled down after publication, or WITHDRAWN if you cancelled it yourself. Your developer dashboard shows both the state and any review note so nothing ever disappears silently.

Pushing an update follows the same review flow. While your new build is pending, the store keeps serving the previous approved version so an unreviewed or broken upload never breaks existing installs. When a user updates, the new package installs cleanly over the old one while keeping all stored extension data.

Everything powering the website and app is served from https://api.kodanetwork.eu. Public read endpoints don't require an API key: GET /v1/status live numbers (servers, players, store, tunnel server) GET /v1/releases published app releases GET /v1/servers the public server directory (name, status, players, MOTD, owner) GET /v1/servers/{host}?ping=1 one server: owner, and a live minecraft ping (players, MOTD, favicon) GET /v1/extensions the catalog, approved only, with the newest version GET /v1/extensions?author=Name everything one publisher released GET /v1/extensions/{id} one extension with all approved versions GET /v1/extensions/{id}/download redirects to a 60 second signed url Authenticated routes expect your Supabase session access token as a Bearer header (the exact same login the web dashboard uses): GET /v1/me profile, nickname, avatar url, counters, 2FA state PATCH /v1/me nickname and avatar POST /v1/me/avatar upload target for a profile picture GET /v1/me/devices linked devices with their telemetry and MC accounts POST /v1/me/devices/{id}/unlink detach a device; the app keeps working standalone GET /v1/me/extensions your submissions with their review state GET /v1/me/tickets your support tickets POST /v1/me/tickets/{id}/messages reply to a ticket from the browser When a public server is reachable, the detail endpoint performs a real Minecraft server-list ping and returns live players, MOTD, and server favicon (cached for one minute). Public listings only ever expose the owner's linked Minecraft username, never app UUIDs, tokens, or hardware IDs. Two things stay off the public API deliberately: the personal support chat is end-to-end encrypted between the Android app and admin app, so it only lives inside the app. And extension packages never get static public URLs; every download redirects to a signed link that expires after 60 seconds, keeping pending or rejected uploads unreachable. All routes sit behind database-backed sliding-window rate limits (120 reads per minute per IP, 30 writes, 90 per account, and 20 for ticket replies and uploads), shared consistently across edge instances. If you hit a limit, the API returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, and the site displays a calm cooldown screen with a countdown instead of throwing cryptic errors.

Every piece of UI copy lives in app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml, with built-in translations right alongside it in values-de, values-zh-rCN, and values-pl. Because Android falls back to the default file for any missing entry, you can start with a partial translation and fill in the rest over time. Adding a new built-in language just means creating its resource directory and wiring it into the language picker in settings. Two scripts keep everything safe: python3 extensions/tools/check_translation.py app/src/main/res/values-pl/strings.xml python3 extensions/tools/check_language_pack.py path/to/lang/es.json Always run the checker after editing strings. A broken format placeholder looks totally innocent in XML, then crashes the app at runtime the moment that text gets rendered.

Under the hood, the app starts from Material 2 with an opt-in Material 3 mode that derives a full colour scheme from a single seed. In Material 3 mode, the theme helper resolves all colour roles once and applies them across the view tree, which is also the hook extension themes plug into. Base palettes live in colors_m3.xml alongside its night variant. In Classic mode, views use fixed colours and extension palettes map onto those slots. Whenever you want a colour change to ripple cleanly across the entire app, make it in the theme helper instead of hunting through individual layouts.

index.t: Layout variants, and the trap that keeps biting
index.h: Layout variants, and the trap that keeps biting
index.x: Core screens ship with multiple layout variants: Classic, Material 3, Sleek, and a Terminal layout for the server screen. Because activities choose their layout dynamically at runtime, adding a new view means either adding it to every layout variant or writing defensive lookups when a variant omits it. This one bit us in production before: a settings card was added only to the classic layout, which threw a null pointer crash in Material 3 mode, locking users out of the very settings screen where they could switch themes back. Keep this two-line habit everywhere: View card = findViewById(R.id.card_my_feature); if (card == null) return; // this layout variant may not have it card.setOnClickListener(v -> openMyFeature());

Icons, the K monogram, and brand colours live in branding/ and are generated via script, so updating an asset means editing one source instead of twenty PNGs. Interface typography uses font_koda and logs/code use font_koda_mono, with their license files tracked right alongside all third-party licenses. Minecraft server jars and Java runtimes are never bundled inside the APK. Downloading and verifying them on demand keeps the install tiny and keeps licensing clean. The app only ships its own assets, bundled server-side helper plugins, and license notices.

A handful of simple rules keep the app feeling cohesive, and breaking them sticks out immediately once you spend ten minutes using it: Stick to the Koda palette instead of inventing random greys. Orange highlights actions, green signals online health, and red warns of danger. Keep buttons and cards at a 12 dp corner radius on flat surfaces without heavy drop shadows. Ship every new UI string in English, German, Chinese, and Polish. Keep utility sheets focused: clear controls and one clear outcome, not walls of text. When adding a step to an existing flow, match the layout of that flow rather than inventing a second style.

index.t: Adding a screen or a setting
index.h: Adding a screen or a setting
index.x: New screens are plain Android activities paired with XML layouts, wired up directly with findViewById and click listeners. Skipping a heavy navigation framework keeps each screen self-contained and easy to read on its own. To add a new setting, mirror an existing card in both settings layouts and wire it up in the settings activity, or inject it dynamically the same way extension rows work. To add a new native server tab, extend the tab list and panel handler (extension server tabs do the exact same thing programmatically, so they're a great reference to follow).

The control plane runs on Supabase with a deliberately small, easy-to-audit schema. Raw tables stay locked off from direct API access; every action a client is allowed to take goes through an explicit database function. Table What it stores koda_users one row per device: app UUID, device token, linked Minecraft account, nickname, permissions, and ban state koda_servers one row per server: owner, software type, version, port, join address, live state, and join address history koda_ports the shared port pool, allocated and freed exclusively by edge functions releases app releases with changelog copy, channel, banner artwork, and publish flag app_settings remote flags: maintenance mode, minimum supported versions, and feature toggles support_tickets, support_ticket_messages support tickets and reply threads, plus the encrypted personal chat extension_* the extension registry: packages, versions, review state, and reports Naming stays strictly consistent: client-callable RPCs start with rpc_, while internal database helpers start with fn_. Read RPCs stand in for direct table queries, and every write RPC verifies the caller's device token inside the function itself instead of blindly trusting request parameters.

Lightweight Deno edge functions handle everything that requires private credentials or server-side authority: allocating and releasing ports, checking server name availability, creating and deleting DNS records, provisioning Java runtimes, and handing out tunnel configs once a device token checks out. Edge functions are the only layer that holds external service secrets. Incoming requests pass the app UUID and device token, and a single shared helper in supabase/functions/_shared handles caller verification consistently across every endpoint.

KodaDash is a compact Java plugin that spins up its own HTTP server using the JDK's built-in server classes, so it carries zero third-party dependencies beyond the Minecraft plugin API. Each area registers its own clean handler: console, players, files, settings, plugins, logs, backups, schedules, stats, efficiency, and server actions. The console handler is where the cleverness lives: it attaches a Log4j appender via a dynamic proxy, maintains a bounded per-client queue on a dedicated writer thread, and tags every streamed event with a monotonically increasing line index. If your browser disconnects when your phone sleeps, it reconnects and picks up on the exact line it missed. To avoid race conditions, KodaDash never overwrites files owned by the Android app. The app mirrors stats, backups, and schedules into the server directory, and KodaDash treats them as read-only so every piece of state has a single clear owner.

A small Node.js service polls the releases table for anything marked published that hasn't been announced yet. It runs server-side with the service role key, posts the changelog and banner image to Discord, and flips the announced flag afterward so restarting the bot never causes duplicate posts. The bot is strictly an announcer: it never creates or edits releases itself. Publishing stays an explicit button click in the operator admin panel.

The website is a fast static app paired with a live dashboard that talks to the same Supabase backend using the public anon key and standard user login. It focuses on the things a phone screen isn't great for: viewing all your servers side by side, reading changelogs comfortably, managing extensions, or checking server status while you're at a desk. Legal notices and third-party license lists come from the exact same source files bundled in the Android app, so fixing a typo once updates both places. These docs live right in the same site and repository as the code they document.

Two private operator tools sit on top of the service role key, which is why neither lives in the public repository: The web admin panel for publishing app releases, uploading release banners, and reviewing extension submissions. The Android admin app for urgent on-the-go operations: user and device bans, support tickets, email tools, DNS management, and server triage. If you self-host your own KodaHosting instance, you can either build lightweight admin tools of your own or manage rows directly in the Supabase dashboard, which works fine for smaller setups.

Yes, the app ships with a public API key, and that's completely intentional because that key alone can't authorize any mutation. Every write carries the device's UUID and a per-installation device token, and server-side functions verify that exact pair before modifying a single row. Device tokens are randomly generated per installation and rotate automatically whenever a device resets. Row level security stays enabled everywhere, with zero permissive open policies on client tables. Admin functions check an explicit allowlist on top of credentials, so merely possessing a key isn't enough to act as an admin. Anti-tamper checks guard the app's own state and identity, kept intentionally narrow so normal users never hit false positives. Attack simulations live in the repo and continuously test the classic abuse paths using the public key: tokenless writes, privilege escalation, ticket spoofing, and raw table reads. Every one of them has to fail. Server-side plugins keep their credentials separate too. Your KodaDash token lives inside the server folder rather than the app, and even a leaked dashboard token can never delete backups.

The public API runs at https://api.kodanetwork.eu and returns JSON across the board. Public read endpoints used by this website don't require an API key. Everything under /v1/me expects your Supabase access token in an Authorization: Bearer... header. Method and path What it returns GET /v1/status API version, live server and player counts, tunnel load, latest release, and maintenance flag GET /v1/servers?limit=12 public servers with host address, status, MOTD, and player counts GET /v1/servers/{host} single public server details, including a live Minecraft ping when reachable GET /v1/extensions the approved extension store catalog GET /v1/extensions/{ext_id} full extension details, description, screenshots, and approved versions GET /v1/extensions/{ext_id}/download?version={code} redirects to a short-lived signed package download URL GET /v1/invite/{token} details for a server invite, including join addresses and usage limits

Method and path What it does POST /v1/invite/{token}/accept accepts an invite and attaches the shared server to your account GET /v1/me account profile, linked Minecraft account, counters, and 2FA status PATCH /v1/me updates your nickname or avatar URL GET /v1/me/devices linked devices along with telemetry and linked Minecraft accounts POST /v1/me/devices/{app_uuid}/unlink detaches a device from your account GET /v1/me/tickets list of your support tickets and their most recent message GET /v1/me/tickets/{id} full conversation history for a single ticket POST /v1/me/tickets/{id}/messages posts a reply to a ticket GET /v1/me/extensions your extension submissions and their review status POST /v1/extensions, /versions, /finalize, /withdraw the full extension store submission lifecycle POST /v1/assets creates a signed upload URL for an extension icon or screenshot POST /v1/me/servers/{host}/action starts, restarts, or stops a server remotely

Failed requests return { "error": "name" } paired with a standard HTTP status code. A 401 means your session expired and you need to sign in again. A 429 includes a retry_after duration in seconds; the web UI pauses cleanly with a countdown until that window clears rather than dumping raw errors on screen. The extension submission pipeline enforces a few extra invariants: version_code must strictly increase, only one version per extension can sit in review at once, and package SHA-256 hashes are always verified post-upload. The live status page links straight here so real-time metrics and their exact API endpoints stay connected.

Development splits across two repositories: a private day-to-day repo and a public mirror. A dedicated mirror script copies tracked source files, filters out local helper scripts, IDE files, and database backups, and scans every file for private instance data before pushing. If an unfamiliar secret-like pattern shows up, the push aborts automatically. That safety net is what makes publishing a codebase this size sustainably possible. Branching stays lightweight: features happen on short-lived branches, releases get tagged, and the public mirror gets clean snapshot commits. If you fork the project, you can use the exact same publish script to protect your own instance secrets.

index.t: The checks that run around a change
index.h: The checks that run around a change
index.x: None of these checks exist just to pad a CI badge. Every single one was added after that exact mistake actually made it onto a phone at least once: Check What it catches./gradlew:app:testDebugUnitTest manifest validation rules, example extensions that must install cleanly on the current build, and archive path traversal check_language_pack.py typo keys in extension language packs that would otherwise silently do nothing check_translation.py built-in translations with missing keys or mismatched format placeholders Koda Lab on a real device live bridge behaviour, raw JSON responses, storage quotas, and rate limits Extension packaging tools unknown view IDs, missing files, and invalid colour codes before a package leaves your machine Mirror publish script accidental instance config or credentials before anything hits the public repository

Shipping a release means bumping the version, building signed artifacts, creating a row in releases, and uploading a banner. The order matters because the app checks the database for updates rather than relying on the store listing alone. Increment versionCode and versionName in Gradle, then build a signed app bundle for Google Play and a signed APK for direct downloads. Insert a draft entry in releases with the changelog, channel, and banner image, keeping it unpublished while you double-check everything. Flip the published flag: the in-app update prompt starts offering the new build, and the Discord bot announces it automatically. Anyone running an older build sees your changelog right inside the update screen, so write changelogs for real humans rather than dumping raw git commit messages.

KodaHosting is free software released strictly under the GNU General Public License v3. Source files carry a short header pointing to the full license text. If you fork the code and distribute your build, keep those headers and the GPLv3 terms intact so your users get the exact same freedoms you received. Third-party libraries and licenses are published in two places on purpose: inside the app under Settings, Licenses, and online at host.kodanetwork.eu/licenses.html so anyone can inspect them before installing. Whenever you add a new dependency, make sure its license lands there too. Extensions are separate works that talk to KodaHosting over its documented bridge API, so they aren't forced under GPLv3. Every extension picks and declares its own license, which the app surfaces clearly to users. That's why license is required in every manifest and why the store strongly encourages linking source code.

Most hiccups have a straightforward cause, and the app usually points you right to it before you have to dig: Symptom Where to look first Server starts and immediately stops open the console tab; the crash card identifies the cause and usually offers a one-tap fix Friends can't connect verify the live join address on the dashboard and make sure the server actually shows online Server dies when the screen turns off check Android battery optimization settings; the app needs background exemptions enabled Downloads keep failing check the network alarm and open the verbose app log under Log in the console tab An update isn't showing up check your installed version in Settings and confirm the release is marked published A newly added plugin breaks startup head to the plugins tab, toggle off the newest jar, and check the console again Still stuck? Open the debug log screen and attach everything to a support ticket in one tap. That gives way more context than trying to describe the error from memory.

index.h: Does my server keep running when I close the app?
index.x: Yes. Servers run inside an Android foreground service with a persistent notification, and onboarding walks you through battery exemptions so Android doesn't put it to sleep. You can still watch the console and manage everything through KodaDash while the phone screen is off.

index.h: Do I have to create an account?
index.x: Nope. Hosting works completely without an account. Creating one simply adds the web dashboard, easy recovery on a new phone, and family sharing permissions.

index.h: Are my worlds uploaded to the cloud?
index.x: Never. Your world files stay locally on your phone unless you explicitly initiate a device-to-device transfer, and even then they travel encrypted straight between your two phones.

index.h: Why isn't the app available on the Play Store for every phone or country?
index.x: Running a real Minecraft server takes solid RAM and a modern Android WebView. Keeping store eligibility honest prevents people with unsupported devices from running into crashes and frustration.

index.h: Can I host more than one server at the same time?
index.x: Yes, as long as your phone has the memory for it. The app monitors your combined RAM budget automatically, and you can hibernate worlds you aren't playing so they take zero memory or battery.
Open a support ticket right inside the app or drop into the Discord server. And for personal stuff that has nothing to do with Minecraft servers, the encrypted personal chat is always there too.
